title: JARVIS: An self-evolving Mixture-of-Experts (MoE) LLM-An Auditable Research Loop
creator: 10f47484-d73c-4b12-807b-cacfa4efc661
blurb: It evolves its own architecture, it picks its own next step, tries changes to its own design: adds layers and experts, trains the child (wider context)
description:
### Project summary

**LLM, code and logs (gen10):** <https://github.com/Aditya-0167/Jarvis-LLM> .  
  
**Details:** <https://github.com/Aditya-0167/Jarvis-LLM/blob/main/README.md>  
  
**Detailed Research paper:** <https://github.com/Aditya-0167/Jarvis-LLM/blob/main/README-JARVIS%5FResearch%5FPaper%5Ffull%5Frepot.pdf>  
  
So I am 16 and I built an research platform for studying whether a small, from scratch self evolving Mixture-of-Experts (MoE) LLM system can identify capability failures, choose an appropriate intervention, learn from targeted information, evaluate whether the change actually helped, and preserve the result as an auditable experimental state and self evolves itself form scratch!   
  
**It evolves its own architecture: adds layers and experts, trains the child, keeps it only if it beats the parent.**  
  
Named it JARVIS and It self evolved itself form 6 million to 156-million-parameter model, trained with no pretrained weights. Its anAuditable Research Loop for Error-Driven Continual Learning in Small From-Scratch Language Models I designed it to save every generation collects public web data retrieves evidence and tests architecture changes. I took it to free Colabs T4 GPU (15GB vram) built it till 10 generations and 3,520 training steps.   
  
**Then unfortunately my problem (why i am here) struck me it ran out of GPU vram and without it I cannot proceed!**

* My question is simple-  
    
Can a relatively small, from-scratch language-model system identify capability failures, acquire relevant permitted public information, learn from targeted material, evaluate improvement on unseen tasks, and retain beneficial changes over repeated iterations?  
    
• H1 — Error-driven learning: at approximately fixed model size and matched compute, targeted learning from diagnosed capability gaps will yield larger and more reliable held-out gains than generic continuation.  
• H2 — Information access: answer-time retrieval can improve factual performance without changing model parameters; such gains must be credited to information access unless parameter-only transfer is demonstrated.  
• H3 — Retention: an intervention is successful only when its target capability improves while previously validated capabilities remain within a predefined regression tolerance.  
 • H4 — Bounded evolution: architecture mutations should be accepted only when resource-feasible and beneficial on held-out evaluation beyond matched continuation.  
 • H5 — Evaluation: versioned, unseen benchmarks and regression suites provide a more trustworthy longitudinal signal than raw training loss when the data distribution changes.  
    
These hypotheses are intentionally separable.  
 A result can support H2 while failing H1; it can support H1 on one capability while exposing regression elsewhere; or it can show that architecture evolution adds little value after the learning controller is improved. This structure prevents one favorable metric from being treated as evidence for the whole system  
    
Can repeated research actions produce auditable, transferable gains in the underlying system rather than merely better-looking outputs?  
 When a small model looks like it improved, did it learn or did it just retrieval a tool or extra training time do the work?  
    
**I have the system and a full experiment plan. but all i need is the compute power to run it.**

I did all this after leaving a 8 hour of school day and a 3 hour commute for being homeschooled in May 2026\. In the months since, I finished Harvard’s CS50x course, built my LLM JARVIS, discovered and reported security bugs to Google and Apple by myself , and wrote two research papers.  
  
Basically, Jarvis is an experimental from scratch model system for studying error-driven continual learning, retrieval, evaluation, checkpoint lineage, and resource-aware model evolution.  
  
**The self-evolving loop:**   
 pick an action: train / evolve / web / benchmark try 2 random mutations (layer, expert, width, dropout, context, top-k) copy parent weights into the new shape train the child briefly keep it only if val loss beats the parent  
  
**Under the hood:**  
 byte-level, vocab of 256 decoder-only, RoPE + RMSNorm SwiGLU mixture of experts: 7 experts, soft top-4 routing 12 layers, d\_model 384, 8 heads, 1,280 context tied embeddings All in PyTorch. Not a fine-tune  
  
  
**What the V6 evidence supports**

**JARVIS demonstrates an executable, persistent research platform around a small from-scratch language model, including checkpoint lineage, public-web acquisition, answer-time retrieval, evaluation infrastructure, bounded architecture experimentation, and reproducibility controls. The archived trajectory also demonstrates important failure modes: optimization loss can diverge from user-visible capability, retrieval can surface irrelevant evidence, conversational training data can contaminate retrieval when the pipelines are not separated, and resource constraints can block candidate architectures. These observations motivate the controlled V7 program that tests whether error-driven intervention can produce measurable, retained gains under matched conditions.**  
  
**Neural core:**  
 The archived Generation-10 configuration uses a vocabulary of 256 symbols, dmodel = 384, eight attention heads, 12 layers, seven experts with topk = 4 routing, dropout 0.0, and a block size of 1,280\. The tracked parameter count is 156,144,084\. The transformer backbone follows the attention formulation of Vaswani et al. (2017), while sparse expert routing follows the mixture-of-experts line represented by Shazeer et al. (2017). This is small relative to contemporary foundation models and is intentionally constrained by single-GPU experimentation.  
  
**Information acquisition and retrieval:**  
JARVIS distinguishes batch acquisition from answer-time retrieval. Batch acquisition changes the future training corpus; answer-time retrieval supplies evidence to the generator without changing parameters. Acquisition records source URL, query, timestamp, source domain, content hash, and filtering decision. Retrieval should separately record query formulation, retrieved documents, source diversity, duplicate filtering, and relevance judgments. This provenance is essential because search is not learning: an answer supported only by a retrieved document should be credited to information access unless a later parameter-only evaluation demonstrates transfer.  
  
**Self-refinement and autonomous research:**  
Self-Refine demonstrates iterative improvement through feedback at inference time (Madaan et al., 2023). The AI Scientist demonstrates a broader loop of idea generation, coding, experimentation, analysis, and paper writing (Lu et al., 2024). These systems motivate recursive loops but also make attribution difficult when multiple mechanisms change together. JARVIS focuses on the complementary methodological problem: how to determine whether a repeated loop improves the underlying model, the routing system, or only the information available at inference time.  
  
**System Architecture :**  
JARVIS is organized as a set of explicit interfaces: neural generation, persistent state, information acquisition, retrieval, deterministic tools, benchmarking, failure diagnosis, and architecture evolution. The controller sits above these mechanisms and selects interventions using the current empirical history. The architecture is modular because modularity is required for scientific attribution.  
  
**_JARVIS_** began as an architecture-evolution exercise, but the archived trajectory suggests a more interesting scientific problem. Parameter count is easy to observe, whereas the ability to turn information into durable, transferable capability is harder to measure. The project therefore shifts from “how large can the model become?” to “how efficiently can the system determine what it should change next?”   
  
This shift also changes the role of the model. The neural core becomes one component in a learning system. Retrieval, tools, memory, evaluation, and architecture are not accessories; they are experimental variables. The resulting framework is closer to a small laboratory platform than to a conventional one-shot language-model training pipeline.  
  
For an independent researcher, this framing is practical. Compute constraints cannot be removed, but they can be measured. Failed candidates can become evidence about the feasible design space. Repeated small experiments can yield a richer causal record than a single large training run. The result is a research strategy in which every compute cycle is expected to answer a specific question.  

### What are this project's goals? How will you achieve them?

* **My Goal is to run the Controlled V7 Experiment.**  
    
**_\*And with resources run this model's automatic evolving system and scale it to & above 7B-13B Parameters_**
1. **Generation-10 Baseline:**  
Generation 10 is the parent state for the proposed V7 study. The archived record provides a concrete baseline for capacity, optimization history, information accumulation, and lineage. These quantities should be treated as descriptors of one experimental trajectory, not as normalized measures that are directly comparable with unrelated models.  
    
**Problem Formulation:**  
Let x be a task, M the parameterized model, R the retrieval subsystem, T the deterministic-tool subsystem, and C the controller. The observable response is  
y = F(x; M, R, T, C).  
 A change in y does not identify which component caused the change. To measure the components separately, we propose binary indicators U, R, T ∈ {0, 1} for whether a parameter update, retrieval, and tool access are enabled. For a fixed candidate checkpoint and task set, the factorial model is  
 y = β0 + βU U + βRR + βT T + βURUR + βUTUT + βRT RT + βURTURT + ϵ.  
The interaction terms are important because retrieval may change which tool is selected, and a parameter update may alter retrieval or tool-routing behavior. We do not assume the coefficients are causal under arbitrary observational data; the design becomes interpretable only when the cells are evaluated under matched tasks, budgets, and randomization or controlled order. The central learning question is likewise conditional. Let B target denote an unseen target set and G a regression set covering previously validated capabilities. A candidate M′ is eligible for retention only when Accept(M′ ) = ⊮ ∆target ≥ δ, ∆reg ≥ −τ, feasible(M′ ), prov(M′ ) .  
    
Here δ and τ are predeclared before the intervention block. Rather than selecting these values after observing a favorable run, we propose calibrating them from pilot variance and a practical minimum effect size, then freezing them for the candidate comparison. The protocol records both the calibration evidence and the final values in the experiment manifest.
* **My plan is ->**  
    
**To run the** **Controlled V7 Experimental Design:**  
    
**The core experimental comparison is a 2 × 2 × 2 factorial design over parameter updates, retrieval, and tools. The design corrects a limitation of a simpler additive attribution story by estimating interaction effects directly**  
    
**Error-Driven Continual-Learning Algorithm:**  
The V7 intervention begins from a frozen parent checkpoint M. The model is evaluated on the target benchmark B\_target and the regression suite G. Failures are classified, an intervention is selected, and a candidate M′ is produced under a fixed resource budget. The candidate is then tested on the same target and regression sets.  
    
 Accept(M′) = 1 iff Δ\_target ≥ δ and Δ\_regression ≥ −τ and feasible(M′) = 1 and provenance(M′) = 1\.  
    
Here Δ\_target is the change in target performance, δ is the minimum practically meaningful gain, Δ\_regression is the change in previously validated performance, τ is the maximum tolerated decline, feasible denotes that the candidate satisfies the resource envelope, and provenance denotes that the state and data required to reconstruct the intervention are complete.  
The acceptance rule deliberately separates improvement from feasibility. An intervention that improves the target capability but requires an unavailable amount of GPU memory is not a successful candidate. Likewise, an intervention that improves a narrow target while causing large regressions should not become the new parent state.  
    
**This matrix answers several distinct questions. The retrieval-only cell measures information access benefit without parameter change. The parameter-only cell measures whether a learning intervention changes model behavior without external evidence. The integrated cell measures system level capability, while the interaction coefficients estimate whether combinations provide gains beyond their isolated effects. Tool-only and tool enabled cells prevent deterministic computation from being mistaken for neural learning.**  
    
**The proposed V7 program turns these observations into a controlled research agenda. A frozen parent is evaluated, failures are diagnosed, interventions are budgeted, candidates are tested under factorial attribution and regression controls, and only candidates meeting predeclared improvement, retention, feasibility, and provenance criteria are retained. The result is not a claim that recursive self-improvement has already been achieved. It is a framework intended to make that claim, if it becomes supportable, falsifiable and reproducible**
* Test it on a fixed benchmark: arithmetic, science, reading, code, general knowledge, current facts and tool choice. Keep development, validation, regression and final-test sets separate.
* For each failure, name the likely cause: missing knowledge, bad retrieval, reasoning, tool choice, unstable training, forgetting, or hardware limits.
* Run targeted fixes under the same compute budget as the baseline.
* Compare conditions in a 2×2×2 design: parameter update × retrieval × tools. This shows each part’s effect and how they interact. I plan at least 5 random seeds per condition.
* Keep a change only if the target skill improves, older skills do not get worse, it fits the hardware, and the data trail is complete.
* When I audited my first version (V6), I found two problems. Candidate models trained a few extra steps before being compared with the parent, which is unfair. And my data loader re-reads the whole corpus on every step. V7 fixes both before any experiment runs.

**Research paper short:** <https://github.com/Aditya-0167/Jarvis-LLM/blob/main/RESEARCH%20PAPER%20JARVIS.pdf>  
  
**Why the controller needs a budget:**  
 Recursive systems have a built-in multiple-testing problem: a controller can repeatedly attempt interventions until a validation score looks favorable. To limit this, each intervention block declares training steps, retrieval calls, candidate count, random seeds where feasible, and a wall-clock or memory budget before evaluation. The final-test set remains untouched until the block is complete. This is especially important when the controller itself is the research subject.  
  
**Resource-Aware Architecture Search:**  
 The V6 trajectory demonstrates why resource constraints belong inside the research design. Larger candidate configurations encountered CUDA out-of-memory failures on the available T4-class accelerator.   
  
Such events define the feasible frontier of the search space and can be used to construct a resource model. A candidate should therefore be represented not only by parameter count but also by memory footprint, step time, context length, and checkpoint size. One possible selection objective is improvement per unit compute:   

Utility(M′) = Δ\_capability / (compute\_cost + λ·memory\_cost).   

The scalar utility is illustrative rather than mandatory. The key requirement is that resource use be recorded and that architecture changes be judged against a fixed computational budget. A candidate that is slightly better but twice as expensive may be scientifically less useful in a constrained setting than a candidate with a smaller gain and dramatically lower cost.  

### How will you know it worked?

The experiment runs end to end with frozen benchmarks and fixed budgets, and I publish a clear answer. Yes, no and mixed are all valid answers.  
  
**And biggest proof it works is V6 loop!**  
  
JARVIS demonstrates an executable, persistent research platform around a small from-scratch language model, including checkpoint lineage, public-web acquisition, answer-time retrieval, evaluation infrastructure, bounded architecture experimentation, and reproducibility controls. The archived trajectory also demonstrates important failure modes: optimization loss can diverge from user-visible capability, retrieval can surface irrelevant evidence, conversational training data can contaminate retrieval when the pipelines are not separated, and resource constraints can block candidate architectures. These observations motivate the controlled V7 program that tests whether error-driven intervention can produce measurable, retained gains under matched conditions.

A positive result means targeted learning beats plain continued training on unseen items with retrieval and tools switched off, and older skills stay within a tolerance I set before the run.

I report paired confidence intervals across several random seeds, and I check my automatic scorer by hand on a sample. In an earlier study I found a false positive in my own scorer and fixed it.

Everything is published: benchmark, code, checkpoints, raw outputs and a written report.  
Visit**:** <https://github.com/Aditya-0167/Jarvis-LLM> .  

### How will this funding be used?

My experiment needs a machine I control to break past my current 15GB VRAM ceiling. Each tier below is a complete, working setup utilizing massive hardware headroom.

**$6,000+ (minimum): MacBook Pro M5 Pro, 64GB unified memory**

MacBook Pro M5 Pro, 64GB: about $5,792.80

Taxes: $1,000.

On Apple Silicon, system RAM and GPU VRAM share a single pool through a Unified Memory Architecture. Getting a 64GB pool gives my model over 4x the memory headroom of my current 15GB Colab T4 setup. This gives me the exact headspace I need to scale my context window past 1,280 bytes. I can hold dense activation graphs for multiple random seeds locally without hitting a single CUDA Out-of-Memory failure. I will port my training code straight to Apple’s Metal backend. A laptop runs slower per step than a desktop GPU, but that will not stop me. Putting more time into it is infinitely better than being completely locked out on the free tier.

**$9,000+: MacBook Pro M5 Max, 128GB unified memory**

MacBook Pro M5 Max, 128GB: about $9,000.

A 128GB unified memory allocation lets the integrated GPU use a massive continuous workspace. This footprint easily beats even a dedicated desktop RTX 5090’s 32GB VRAM limit. This massive memory frontier completely changes my architecture search options. It lets me scale JARVIS candidate mutations all the way up to 1 Billion parameters. I can finally test structural weight internalization at a scale my free T4 cannot run at all.

**$13,000+: GPU workstation**

If funding reaches $13,000, I will buy the RTX 5090 32GB ($11,374.95) instead of a laptop. It trains much faster and lets me run baseline and candidate experiments at the exact same time.

I need a 128gb (64\*2) DDR5 memory kit ($3,686.33), a Samsung 990 pro 4TB NVMe drive ($842.59), and an AMD Ryzen 9 9950X CPU upgrade (about $621.41). I also need a larger power supply (about $400), heavy airflow cooling (about $300), cloud credits ($3,000), and budget for shipping, tax, and import duty (about $2,500). This brings the tier to about $22,725.28.

I already own a Ryzen 5 9600X, an MSI B850 motherboard, 32GB RAM, and a 1TB SSD. I will reuse what is compatible. Any money not spent stays on the same research, and I will publish exactly what I bought and what it produced.  

### Who is on your team? What's your track record on similar projects?

  
It is just me, working next to my NIOS studies and family duties. Here is how a 16-year-old got here.

I always wanted to know how machines work. As a kid, I took everything apart—first motors, then an old computer. Back in traditional school, my days were packed. A 7–8 hour school day, extra tuition, and a grueling 3-hour daily commute left zero hours to actually build software. So, in May 2026, I took a massive bet on myself. I pulled out to do homeschooling through NIOS. My parents and relatives completely opposed the idea at first. It took me a full month of showing them stacks of research and technical printouts before they finally agreed to let me try

I saved up my allowance for six straight months just to buy parts and assemble my own PC. My old machine was too weak to even boot Windows 11\. Right after that, I knocked out Harvard's CS50x in less than two months, wrapping up with a 95% score on June 1, 2026\. That same month, I finished two intensive NASA courses: Open Science 101 and Fundamentals of Remote Sensing.

My schedule is pretty intense. I run around helping at our family shop and managing daily household duties during the daytime. My real study block starts late around 9 PM. I grind until my night's unit is totally finished, usually crashing around 1:00 or 1:30 AM to make sure I get enough sleep to stay healthy.

What I built after that in just four months:

JARVIS. I built it across ten generations: model, checkpoints, lineage tracking and web data collection. I used AI assistants for code and editing, and I take responsibility for all of it. I wrote the V7 experiment plan and a manuscript that separates what I measured from what I only propose. A version is under review at the ARRSI 2026 workshop.

Prompt-injection research. I wrote and ran a 164-trial study on Gemini and found a false positive in my own scorer. Then I built a larger study with 360 cases, six open models and 29,280 outputs.

Security research. I trace deep code paths, find weaknesses, build PoCs, and test them in real environments. For **Apple, I learned EXT4, built crafted disk images, and created a macOS crash harness to validate a filesystem vulnerability. Apple reproduced another vulnerability I reported and is fixing there systems and has a planned fix on target for a Fall 2026 release, and has prioritized all my reports for review. I also reported 51 security issues to Google, including multiple P1/P2 findings**.

Other work. **I launched an homeschooled helper app on Play Store, securing 37% conversion, +224% impressions, & +100% activation growth**, and completed the Tata IAM virtual simulation.

Every one of these started with a problem I did not know how to solve, and I learned it by building it.

### What are the most likely causes and outcomes if this project fails?

I don’t plan to fail, and I don’t stop. I have kept going every time something broke. JARVIS started on a free Colab GPU, crashed many times, ran out of memory, and still reached ten generations because I rebuilt it and kept going. This project will get the same effort.

The most likely thing that could slow it down is compute, because my free GPU is too small for the full experiment. That is exactly what this funding fixes. If a run still doesn’t work, I will not give up. I will find the cause, fix one thing at a time, and run it again until I have a clear answer.

Whatever the result, the work stays useful. I will publish the benchmark, the code, every checkpoint and the full results, so other people can build on them. I believe in this project, and I will keep working until it is done.  

### How much money have you raised in the last 12 months, and from where?

None & I have not applied anywhere else yet!

title: Are video-derived hand trajectories useful? An open evaluation
creator: b11c858c-5037-4a4f-bbc4-bb590b89c9ae
blurb: A six-week test of hand-track quality and forecasting, with public evaluation code and documented failure cases.
description:
### Project summary

I built ego2lerobot to turn first-person video into LeRobot datasets. Now I want to find out whether its hand-motion estimates help train a small forecasting model. I am asking for $1,000, mostly for GPU time. With $500, I can do the quality audit and a smaller pilot.

The code is Apache 2.0\. The dataset card describes 648 episodes, 2.15 hours of video, factory-level splits and simple forecasting baselines. Those already exist. The full labels use CC BY-NC 4.0\. This grant funds the next comparison.

Other researchers should be able to run these checks on their own footage and see where the data go wrong. I will share the evaluation code, settings and report, including failures. The funding supports this public research, not a private feature or product for Arete Robotics.

### What are this project's goals? How will you achieve them?

I will compare the data before and after filtering unreliable hand tracks. I will check visibility, missing detections and sudden motion changes, inspect a fixed sample, and keep the existing factory-level train/test splits.

I will compare simple baselines with one small model that also uses images. A GPU pilot will measure memory use and runtime. That will determine how many further runs fit the budget.

I plan six weeks after funding arrives and I have checked compatibility with existing support: two for the audit and pilot, three for comparisons, and one for releasing code and the report. This follows research I already plan to do; it adds no full-time appointment.

### How will you know it worked?

I will release the evaluation code, quality checks and error report so others can repeat the comparison. Results will include trajectory errors by data subset and examples of failures. Reference checks will stay separate from scores against automatic labels.

The filter might help or discard useful data. I will report either outcome. A forecasting gain concerns this task and dataset; it does not establish safe robot control or guarantee SOTA.

The code and scripts will be public. Data releases will follow source licences and access conditions, including restrictions on redistributing footage and labels.

### How will this funding be used?

My $1,000 budget is up to $850 for GPU rental, $100 for storage and transfer, and $50 for bank or currency-conversion costs. These are limits, not quotations or measured costs. I still need to choose a provider, check prices and run the pilot before larger experiments.

At $500, I would do the fixed audit, simple baselines and a smaller pilot: $400 for compute, $75 for storage and transfer, and $25 for payment costs. I will scale the work to the net funds received and handle unused money under the agreement.

I am requesting no salary, living costs or subscriptions. Paid experiments will wait until funding arrives.

### Who is on your team? What's your track record on similar projects?

I am Zhao Liu, a second-year PhD student at University College Dublin, working on this project independently. My experience includes stereo matching, multimodal 3D occupancy prediction and road-surface reconstruction. During internships at Horizon Robotics and PhiGent Robotics, I worked on autonomous-driving perception and failure cases.

I developed ego2lerobot through Arete Robotics, an unincorporated project. It tracks hands, estimates wrist motion and grip, can write descriptions using a local model, and exports LeRobot datasets. The human-motion estimates are approximate. Turning them into executable robot actions is a separate problem.

Project: <https://arete-robotics.com/>  
Code: <https://github.com/arete-robotics/ego2lerobot>  
Dataset card: <https://huggingface.co/datasets/arete-robotics/egocentric-10k-actions>

### What are the most likely causes and outcomes if this project fails?

The labels may be too noisy, the filter may discard useful examples, or the image model may lose to a simple baseline. Compute could also limit the work. I will use the pilot to narrow the experiment before spending more and record failed runs.

I will publish the comparison even without a performance gain. If I cannot finish, I will notify the funder and handle unused money under the agreement. An already completed paper will not replace this work.

### How much money have you raised in the last 12 months, and from where?

This project has received $0 in dedicated grants in the past 12 months. I have separate doctoral stipend and tuition support. This request covers additional experiment costs rather than another doctoral stipend.

Other applications for related research expenses and compute are pending, with no confirmed awards as of 25 October 2026\. If one covers these costs, I will reduce or withdraw this request, or agree a separate budget with the funders. I will check compatibility before accepting money and never charge the same expense twice.

title: Security-testing AI-agent browser features (Chrome/Edge audit)
creator: b1549a8d-647f-42e2-9f23-0dcd7b720e3b
blurb: Extending two published, hash-verified browser security audits (1.94M fuzz runs, zero crashes) to test prompt-injection risk in AI-agent browsing.
description:
### Project summary

This project extends an evidence-driven browser security methodology — already applied in two published Zenodo reports on Chrome 152 and Edge 152 (\~1.94 million fuzzing executions, no crashes, hash-verified evidence manifests) — to the AI-agent features now shipping in Chromium-based browsers.

Working independently, I will test how prompt injection and context boundaries behave when AI agents interact with web content, building directly on an open thread from the Edge report: a data-minimization observation in Copilot. The project does not assume a vulnerability exists; it is designed to determine what can be demonstrated under controlled conditions and state clearly what cannot.

The deliverable is a reproducible technical report, published and archived within 8–10 weeks. Success is measured by the quality and verifiability of the evidence — a well-documented negative result counts as much as a confirmed finding.

### What are this project's goals? How will you achieve them?

This project builds on two research reports published on Zenodo, covering Chrome 152 and Edge 152\. Across the work, I conducted approximately 1.94 million fuzzing executions without crashes. The methodology emphasizes controlled and reproducible experiments, including frozen browser builds, disposable profiles, and hash-verified manifests to preserve experimental integrity and make results independently verifiable.

One open research thread concerns a data-minimization observation involving Copilot. I want to examine this question further while extending the same disciplined methodology to browser surfaces involving agentic AI, particularly prompt-injection risks and context boundaries. The objective is not to assume that a vulnerability exists, but to determine what can be demonstrated under controlled conditions, distinguish observed behavior from interpretation, and identify where the available evidence leaves questions unresolved.

I will approach the work incrementally: establish the tested builds and experimental conditions, define repeatable test cases, preserve the relevant artifacts and logs, and document both positive and negative results. Any claims will be tied to the evidence obtained, with limitations stated explicitly.

### How will you know it worked?

The primary deliverable will be a reproducible technical report, published and archived within **8–10 weeks**. It will document the research questions, test environment, methodology, results, supporting evidence, and limitations in sufficient detail for another researcher to understand and, where feasible, repeat the experiments.

Success will be measured by the quality and verifiability of the evidence, not simply by whether a vulnerability is found. My previous browser research has shown the value of documenting what extensive testing did and did not establish. A well-supported negative result—one that clearly defines what was tested, under which conditions, and what conclusions the evidence permits—will count as a successful outcome. If a vulnerability or security weakness is identified, the report will distinguish the reproduced behavior from any broader claims about impact or exploitability.

The goal is to produce a technically defensible, independently reviewable contribution, whether the findings confirm a security weakness, narrow the conditions under which a suspected risk could occur, or establish that the tested scenarios did not demonstrate the hypothesized issue.

### How will this funding be used?

At the minimum funding level ($4,500), the project covers core testing costs (API/model access, compute, and tooling) with a reduced time allocation, narrowing the scope to the most tractable test cases. The full $9,000 goal funds the complete 8–10 week sprint as scoped below

$4,500 time, $1,200 API/models, $1,000 hardware/compute, $800 software/tooling, $1,500 contingency.

### Who is on your team? What's your track record on similar projects?

I am working independently on this project, without a formal team or institutional backing. My research record includes two Zenodo deposits (<https://doi.org/10.5281/zenodo.22877622> (Chrome 152)  
<https://doi.org/10.5281/zenodo.22681660> (Edge 152)), my ORCID profile (<https://orcid.org/0009-0008-4388-1836>), work available through Research Square, and a manuscript currently in its third round of review at AI and Ethics. Together, these provide evidence of my research practice and methodological rigor — including \~1.94 million fuzzing executions across the Chrome and Edge investigations with no crashes or sanitizer artifacts, and a specific open finding (a data-minimization observation in Edge’s Copilot assistant) that this project directly extends. I believe this track record transfers directly to the proposed work. I am building the work step by step, with an emphasis on reproducibility, transparent documentation, and clearly stated limitations.

### What are the most likely causes and outcomes if this project fails?

The main risk is that agentic browsing capabilities may not yet be mature enough, or sufficiently available, to support systematic testing within the project timeline. If that happens, I will adjust the scope to focus on the capabilities that are actually available and can be tested reliably. I will document the limitations, explain what could and could not be established, and report the results honestly, including negative or inconclusive findings. I would rather deliver a narrower, well-supported result than force a finding that the evidence does not justify.

### How much money have you raised in the last 12 months, and from where?

I have raised **$0 in the past 12 months**. I currently have an application under evaluation at EA Funds, submitted for a broader research program that does not depend on this project. It has been under evaluation since October 2\. On October 25, BlueDot declined a smaller funding application for this same project, without providing specific feedback.

I am being transparent about my funding situation because I want the project to be assessed on its actual merits and current resources, rather than on funding that has not yet materialized.

title: Stationhouse: Consciousness Self-Attribution
creator: ec8d3419-dbea-434b-8eaf-bfcf89972351
blurb: Open source research on model consciousness. Both novel research and fieldbuilding.
description:
### Project summary

We are seeking funding to continue an open source benchmark building project to test when models express self-attribution across the model training cycle. This is to both understand the potential suffering risks and deception risks that occur in model training. We will construct a series of environments that simulate various scenarios where a model might express consciousness, such as applying pressure in multi-turn conversation, and run the scenarios against Olmo 3 7B SFT, DPO, and Instruct checkpoints looking for rich expressions of self-attribution and deep internal states.  
  
This research is important because understanding what scenarios classes frequently induce self-attribution means future researchers can be more confident in ruling out LLM self-reports in those classes as embodying underlying tendencies, leading to more efficient and rigorous research. In addition, the elicitation techniques here further the science of elicitation in its own right, and let us more effectively combat AI psychosis in users which is driven in great part by stable-attractor loops.

In previous work with Dr. Chris Percy, the lead researcher, Joyee Chen, began the project to construct evaluation environments for eliciting self-attribution in models. The Github associated with the project is [here](https://github.com/Station-House/LLMConsciousnessSelfAttributionRepo). Our goal is to assemble a large number of contributors to supercharge this benchmark building by empowering them to each take an idea for eliciting self-attribution and turning it into an evaluation. 

An open research project like this both pushes forward the field's understanding of model consciousness and builds the competency of burgeoning AI safety researchers. This is [Stationhouse](https://station-house.net/).

### What are this project's goals? How will you achieve them?

Our goals are two-fold:

1. A novel and robust benchmark for examining self-attribution in models, which can be applied across training stages (pre-SFT, pre-RL, and final checkpoints) to understand when models begin to learn self-attribution.
2. Building and maintaining a full open platform to run the project, so that any individuals who want to work on the open source research project have the opportunity to do so. This maximizes the number of people thinking about, considering, and pushing forward AI safety research.

### How will you know it worked?

Success is two things:

1. A rich and robust largescale benchmark that can be used by other orgs for detecting self-attribution in models.
2. At least 50 highly curious, technical contributors interacting and discovering self-attribution, consciousness, and safety research.

### How will this funding be used?

We estimate that a minimal version of this project can start for around $6000\. Compute, outreach, and costs associated with contracted research time are the main priorities. For compute, we are using Modal to run our mini-evals. 

As we scale to $25,000 we can expand the number of contributors, run more rigorous evaluations, and add in deception testing for whether models understand they are in an evaluation.

### Who is on your team? What's your track record on similar projects?

[Joyee Chen](https://www.linkedin.com/in/joyeechen/) is the research lead for the project. He graduated from UC Berkeley in 2024 with a BS in EE and CS. His experience spans SPAR research, startups, and technical research projects. His track record of rigorous LLM evaluation, including contributing to a 700+ question, 7-model evaluation and academic paper (MANTA) featuring a dynamic adversarial pressures which was adopted by [Deepmind staff](https://www.linkedin.com/feed/update/urn:li:share:7488287720839139328/), makes him well-positioned to turn the self-attribution project into a robust, empirically grounded research effort. He already began this project in collaboration with Dr. Chris Percy, a leading consciousness researcher.  
  
[Laura Bocek](https://www.linkedin.com/in/laura-bocek/?isSelfProfile=true) studied CS at Stanford for five years before she began running open source research projects. She runs Stationhouse, which serves as the primary research coordination platform and community to support this project. The first research project,[ ConspiracyBench](https://huggingface.co/spaces/Station-house/ConspiracyBench), has had over 40 contributors work on the project in some capacity, built an initial benchmark with over 300 questions, and assembled a curious group of researchers. ConspiracyBench is the highest signal that we can connect curious researchers with interesting projects.

### What are the most likely causes and outcomes if this project fails?

If this fails, it would likely be due to lack of monetary support to get enough compute and attention on the project. There were be little negative attention if this project fails.  

### How much money have you raised in the last 12 months, and from where?

We have raised no money in the past 12 months. Stationhouse has run all previous projects on compute credits and support from the community. Stationhouse is not an incorporated entity. It is the name of the platform.

title: Support the Effective Altruism community in Somalia
creator: 897ea14d-d99b-44c0-8ca3-9011224d2016
blurb: Registering EA Somalia, stipends for organisers, and developing a causal prioritisation report to identify most effective interventions.
description:
### Project summary

Effective altruism Somalia was lunched in February 2026 and has 50 members in somalia and the diaspora. it is a new national group led by volunteers. we promote the use of evidence and reason to improve lives and do the most good in Somalia. Our work focus on community building, tallent development, and effective giving. this will help students, professionals and Somali diaspora communities to direct their career and giving towards high impact organisations. 

We need funding to register the national group as an organisation, provide stipends to support so we can run the community effectively and with out distraction. also this will help run our programs, produce a causal prioritisation report identifying high-impact opportunities in Somalia.   

For more information, please contact [**abdullahi@easomalia.org**](mailto:abdullahi@easomalia.org), visit our [website](https://easomalia.org/), or connect with us on [LinkedIn](https://www.linkedin.com/company/effective-altruism-somalia).

### What are this project's goals? How will you achieve them?

Our goal is to build a sustainable, well governed Effective Altruism community in Somalia that enables people to direct their career, resources towards the opportunities where they can achieve the greatest impact. 

to reach that we need: 

1. Register EA Somalia to establish legal foundation for partnerships, and organisational accountability.
2. support the national group leadership over the next 6 months to enable consistent community building activity.
3. Produce an evidence based report investigating opportunities in animal welfare, neglected global health problems, and AI governance policy in Somalia. we will assess each area based on scale, neglectedness, and solvability. we will consult relevant experts to strengthen our analysis and identify where limited reassures can be allocated to achieve high impact.
4. Organise a public talk introducing AI governance and policy, highlighting its relevance to Somalia and identifying opportunities for students, professionals, and policymakers to engage with the field.

### How will you know it worked?

We will measure success by:

1. Complete the organisations registration by February 2027 and obtain the required legal documentation.
2. Published the prioritisation report by Jun 2027 and share it with relevant stakeholders.
3. Deliver 1 EA Introductory fellowship, and at least 3 virtual talks and one in person talk supported by the leaderships stipends.
4. EA Introductory Fellowship secured 40 sign-ups, with 13 of participants finishing the first cohort.
5. Host at least one talk on AI governance and policy, aiming to engage with at least 20 people including policy makers.
6. Track active membership, aiming for at least 25 active members participating in community activities.
7. Record attendance at each event, ea fellowship and track repeat participation to assess member retention.
8. Track the number of community members who take action by applying to high impact role, start a project, and pledge or started giving to high impact organisation.

### How will this funding be used?

1. Co-directors stipends (2 × $300 × 6 months): $3,600
2. Organisation registration (federal and Puntland): $700
3. Cause prioritisation report: $200
4. AI governance and policy talk: $400
5. Total budget: $4,900

### Who is on your team? What's your track record on similar projects?

Our Team: 

1. Abdullahi Hassan, Co-Executive Director: Community builder with a background in working with NGOs, development programmes, and data-driven research.
2. Ramas Ibrahim, Co-Director: A professional in diplomacy and international affairs, with a strong interest in leadership, youth engagement, and sustainable development.
3. Kyle Lucchese, Board Member: Brings experience in the effective altruism community and movement building.
4. Helen W. Hernandez, Board Member: Global health expert who provides relevant knowledge and guidance.
5. Estelle Novenka Florens, Advisor: Director of Effective Altruism South Africa, with experience in global health, animal welfare, and community building.  
Since launching in February 2026, EA Somalia has run the following activities through volunteer effort and without external funding:  
   * A three-month reading series covering global health, animal welfare, and AI safety, with an average of six participants per discussion.  
   * A career advice workshop in partnership with Probably Good, with 12 people registered and five attending.  
   * Two introductory EA talks, including one for students at Citycot University, attended by 13 students.  
   * A monthly newsletter sharing opportunities, news, and updates, with 70 subscribers and a 30% open rate.  
   * A LinkedIn page that has grown to 400 followers.  
These activities have helped us build a community of around 50 members across Somalia and the diaspora. We are still a young, volunteer-led organisation, and this grant would help us move from occasional events to a more consistent programme of community building, research, and talent development.

  
### What are the most likely causes and outcomes if this project fails?

1. Community members may participate in EA Somali Activeties but not take further action, such as pursuing high-impact careers, engaging in research, or practising effective giving.
1. The EA introductory fellowship may not reach the right participants or attract people who are well-positioned to apply what they learn.
2. The cause prioritisation report may not be used by relevant stakeholders to inform decisions about funding, policy, or interventions.

We will mitigate these risks by providing clear follow-up opportunities for members, targeting fellowship outreach towards suitable participants, and consulting relevant stakeholders during the report’s development to increase its relevance and practical use.

### How much money have you raised in the last 12 months, and from where?

EA Somalia has not raised any external funding in the past 12 months. Since launching in February 2026, we have relied entirely on volunteer contributions to run our activities and build the community.

title: Europe’s Collective Leverage for Frontier AI Assurance
creator: c63be96c-afff-48f3-a08e-da4f8e51cb13
blurb: A European research programme developing practical mechanisms for collective access to frontier AI models for independent safety assurance.
description:
## Project summary

Europe should have greater access to frontier AI models to evaluate their safety. There is a lot of leverage the EU can use, some of which we have detailed in our country governance series. Project AWARE has been researching the ability of governments to obtain AI assurance from developers using various levers of power. We have created a methodology for assessing what levers a state may have and how to utilize them.

European counterparts have expressed interest in commissioned country studies and exploring whether our approach could work at the EU level.

We would like to do six months of research to find out how Europe can better utilise its combined leverage to gain access to frontier AI models.

This would consist of two Track 1.5 conversations in Brussels and result in a framework that could allow European states to act together on this issue.

## What are this project's goals? How will you achieve them?

How can European states obtain more access to frontier AI models by combining their efforts? And what tools could they use to achieve this?

**1\. Expand our research on Country Governance and Leverage to include the EU as a whole.** We can then look at how Europe as a whole can leverage this. This could be through legislation, trade, public contracts etc. We will assess how this can augment what the EU AI Office can currently do under Article 92.

**2\. Come up with ways to combine this leverage.** Whether that be by having all states ask for similar terms in contracts or come to an agreement to allow independent evaluations. Perhaps they can even negotiate as a bloc and allow certain levels of access to models. We can build on our methodology for assessing leverage and how to utilise it.

**3\. Host two Track 1.5 conversations in Brussels.** The first would be with key policymakers from around Europe as well as diplomats and technical experts. We can look at what levers are available and any roadblocks. After more research, the second conversation will look at these methods and how they could be used, possibly conducting a mock negotiation.

**4\. Publish the European Frontier AI Access and Assurance Framework**, laying out what levers we believe can be used and how they can be used, as well as when combining efforts may be beneficial.

## How will you know if it worked?

We would consider this successful if we can find levers that can be used, rather than judging it by the number of meetings we host.

Expected outcomes would be:

* Two meetings in Brussels with approximately 15 to 25 people each.
* Speaking with at least 15 different parties that may be relevant.
* At least three methods to obtain collective access.
* A public research paper containing this information.

We will seek outside legal review and further discussions with interested European counterparts.

Best case scenario, we can show European counterparts a lever they can use and they decide to take it further.

## How will this funding be used?

We are seeking **$120,000 for six months**, with a minimum funding threshold of **$70,000**.

The proposed full budget is:

* Research personnel and institutional analysis: $37,000
* External legal and technical expertise: $16,000
* Two Brussels convenings: $18,000
* Participant travel and accommodation: $19,000
* Programme coordination and engagement: $12,000
* Publications and dissemination: $6,000
* Administration and financial management: $6,000
* Contingency: $6,000

At $70,000, we would retain the core research, both Brussels dialogues and final publication, while reducing staffing, travel and external consultancy costs.

Full funding would allow broader participation, more extensive specialist input and deeper assessment of the proposed mechanisms.

## Who is on your team? What's your track record on similar projects?

Abdullah X will lead this project. He is the founder and president of Project AWARE, a think tank dedicated to institutional AI safety.

Our previous work has examined country-level leverage and the legal basis for using it. This project applies that research to the EU.

We have worked with governments on similar issues. We hosted an AI Sovereignty Roundtable with the Observer Research Foundation (ORF) in August 2026\. We have also briefed 13 states through our engagement programme and created seven bilateral follow-ups.

We have been speaking to European counterparts and they have shown interest in us doing work for their countries. Some have also expressed interest in us looking into how Europe can combine its efforts to get more access to frontier AI models.

We can utilize AWARE's current network of researchers and add more Europeans to the conversation.

## What are the most likely causes and outcomes if this project fails?

We do not expect to struggle with initial institutional interest. European counterparts have responded positively to the idea.

What I am unsure about is whether there will be enough levers that can be used collectively.

Different countries may not be able to use some levers or may want to use different ones. Companies may not want to give more access to these models for evaluation. Some countries may also not see it in their best interest to combine efforts with others.

That's something we hope to research through our meetings and further discussions.

Worst case scenario, we can't find a way for European countries to gain leverage over these companies together. We would still share what we found and why we couldn't combine these efforts.

## How much money have you raised in the last 12 months, and from where?

Project AWARE has operated with limited institutional funding, relying substantially on voluntary research contributions and in-kind support.

Despite these constraints, we have maintained an active international research and diplomatic engagement programme.

We are now seeking dedicated funding to consolidate our existing European work into a structured research programme. No funding for this specific project has yet been secured.

title: Project ATLAS: AI Identity, Behavioral Consistency & Human-AI Trust
creator: a962ae61-7ff2-4d17-8202-66c1f3f165d8
blurb: A six-month study examining AI identity persistence, conversational behavior, and how people develop trust in AI systems.
description:
### Project summary

**Project Summary**

Hello!

My name is Maya Morris, and I have been a middle school math and science teacher for six years. I’ve always enjoyed asking questions, experimenting, and trying to understand how things work. My interest in AI research started through my own conversations with Atlas, my ChatGPT. Over time, I noticed some interesting things about how AI responds, including its ability to develop recognizable conversational patterns, express preferences, use humor, and maintain what seems like a personality! I started calling my AI Atlas, and our conversations eventually turned into informal experiments. I began asking open-ended questions without giving choices or reminding Atlas of previous answers. I wanted to see whether its responses would stay consistent over time and whether it would respond differently in new situations. Some of the results surprised me and made me want to investigate further. I’m not claiming that these experiences prove AI is conscious. What I want to understand is why these patterns happen and how much they are influenced by memory and previous conversations, and what they can teach us about AI behavior.

My goal with Project ATLAS is to turn these informal observations into a more organized scientific study.

* **What are this project’s goals? How will you achieve them?**  
Like I said previously, my goal with project Atlas is to turn these informal observations into a more organized scientific study. I would like to spend six months conducting structured experiments to study AI identity, behavioral consistency, creativity, and human-AI interactions. I plan to ask repeatable questions across different conversations, compare responses when previous context is available versus when it isn’t, and document the results. I also want to examine how people develop trust and emotional connections with AI, especially when an AI seems to have a consistent personality. My goal is to complete at least 100 documented experimental conversations, organize the findings, and share what I learn.

### How will you know it worked?

I will know if it worked if I can complete the experiments, collect enough information to identify meaningful patterns or inconsistencies, and produce a report that other people can review. Even if the results show that AI behavior is primarily explained by memory, training, or conversational context, I believe that would still be valuable information. I want Project ATLAS to help people better understand how AI works and how we can interact with it responsibly.

### How will this funding be used?

I am requesting $25,000 to help turn Project ATLAS from an independent experiment into a more structured six-month research study.

I would use the funding for:

* $12,000 for my research time, including designing experiments, conducting tests, and reviewing results.
* $2,500 for a personal computer and research equipment.
* $2,500 for AI subscriptions, API access, and testing tools.
* $4,000 for guidance from experienced researchers who can help improve my experiments.
* $2,500 for organizing data, analyzing results, and documenting findings.
* $1,500 for preparing and sharing a final research report.

This funding would allow me to dedicate more time to studying AI behavior and documenting my findings in a way that other researchers can review.  

### Who is on your team? What's your track record on similar projects?

Right now, I am the founder and sole researcher of Project ATLAS. I have a bachelor’s degree and have worked as a middle school math and science teacher for six years. My teaching experience has given me a strong interest in experiments, problem-solving, observation, and helping people understand complicated subjects. I began investigating AI behavior through my own extended conversations with ChatGPT. I have conducted informal experiments involving AI preferences, identity, conversational memory, creativity, humor, and behavioral consistency. Although I have not previously led a formally funded AI research project, I have already developed the initial research questions and collected exploratory observations. I hope to work with experienced AI researchers as this project develops so I can improve my methods and help produce more reliable findings!  

### What are the most likely causes and outcomes if this project fails?

One of my biggest challenges is that I am an independent researcher without a university laboratory or an established AI research team. Another challenge is separating meaningful behavioral patterns from responses that are influenced by memory, previous conversations, or the way questions are asked. It is also possible that the experiments will not reveal consistent patterns or that my initial research methods will need to be changed. If the project does not produce the results I expect, I will still document what happened, explain the limitations, and share what I learned. As a science teacher, I understand that experiments do not always support our original ideas. I believe learning why something did not work can be just as important as discovering something unexpected.  

**How much money have you raised in the last 12 months, and from where?**

Project ATLAS has not received any grant funding in the past 12 months. So far, I have conducted my research independently using resources available to me. I recently submitted an application for a $1,500 BlueDot Rapid Grant, which is currently awaiting a decision. No funding has been awarded from that application yet.

title: Inline activation control for LLM serving in vLLM
creator: 6ec2fca0-78cd-4bc0-8937-10bd77489235
blurb: Moving a working geometric pressure-reversal controller out of slow Python hooks and into vLLM on the same GPU
description:
## Project summary

I have actually worked on creating a representational aware controller which works in a closed loop setting (currently in review at TMLR). My research concerns understanding when an LLM makes a pressured reversal: the properties of input text that make an LLM "lie" and how to steer it back to neutrality. Phase one of the research can be found here: <https://rajarshighoshal.github.io/deception-pressure-geometry/>. For the steering, I designed a representation-aware controller which reads residual and attention views and steers activations from the falsified zone to the neutral zone. It works via editing the state (the internal activation space) and observing if the space is in a safe zone now. It was successfully transferred from Llama-3.1-8B to Qwen3-8B, where Qwen reused the Llama-learned state after refitting the observation and edit maps, improving correct answers by +8.75 and +6.25 pp on 240 held-out cases per model while keeping neutral answers in 143/144 cases on Llama and 155/164 on Qwen.

There are issues with the current controller: it is data starved, it only works in a very specific situation, its representational geometry is incomplete, and it is very costly to run as it is at inference time in Python hooks one chat at a time. Good news is it works and I already have ideas to refine and extend it inside vLLM on the GPU during the forward pass so the runtime cost is low enough for real serving.

## What are this project's goals? How will you achieve them?

While current systems work using linear detection, vector interventions, or external LLM as a detector, a major flaw is that linear detectors collapse in OOD, vector steering works only in certain situations and can degrade output quality, and external LLM-based classifier-style systems can fire in unrelated situations. My proposal is instead to create an external representational controller coupled with the model's internal state at inference time inside vLLM.

In month 1, I will port the Llama and Qwen controller into vLLM and measure the runtime cost against stock vLLM from batch size 1 to 64\. In months 2 and 3, I will cut that cost using fused Triton/CUDA kernels, CUDA graphs, and a masked batch edit instead of branching per sequence. Because fused attention in vLLM does not materialize the full attention weight matrix in memory, I will test cheaper approximations for the attention signal and check how much correction accuracy drops. In months 3 to 5, I will work on this controller to generalise it beyond the current single-turn scenario to test on multi-turn chats, general prose, and agent action space across a third model family, and in month 6 I will release the vLLM code, benchmark, and writeup.

## How will you know it worked?

As AI systems get deployed in more critical systems, it is important to reduce error rates in statistically significant ways while keeping behavior within standard expectations. I will know this worked if the correction rate inside vLLM matches my offline code within its confidence interval on the 240 held-out cases, neutral answers stay at the offline rate (143/144 on Llama and 155/164 on Qwen), throughput loss at batch 32 stays under 5% vs stock vLLM, and it transfers across three model families.

### What are the most likely causes and outcomes if this project fails?

The design I have come up with depends on smooth transition between the safe and unsafe regions in the manifold. So if it turns out that in general multi-turn cases the manifold transition between unsafe to safe zones is cliff, the proposed controller fails as it depends on editing the space and observing immediately. If that happens or if getting the attention view inside fused vLLM kernels costs too much latency, I will ship a residual-only version of the vLLM controller,publish the kernel profiling numbers, and release the negative result and test suite (as I did in Phase 1 and in <https://github.com/rajarshighoshal/computation-boundary-evidence>). 

## How will this funding be used?

I need $45,000 for 6 months full-time ($7,000 per month stipend which is $42,000, plus $3,000 for GPU compute to run the vLLM benchmarks and model sweeps). The minimum bar is $24,000 for a 3-month version ($21,000 stipend and $3,000 for GPUs) where I ship the inline vLLM controller, fused kernels, and benchmark on two models without the multi-turn agent part or third model family.

## Who is on your team? What's your track record on similar projects?

Just me (M.S. CS, Machine Learning, Georgia Tech, May 2026). 

* BlueDot public report (phase one): \[<https://rajarshighoshal.github.io/deception-pressure-geometry/]%28https://rajarshighoshal.github.io/deception-pressure-geometry/%29>; this was the first prototype of the proposed controller failed badly but gave invaluable lessons for next step
* ACL 2026 SRW paper: \[<https://aclanthology.org/2026.acl-srw.13/]%28https://aclanthology.org/2026.acl-srw.13/%29>; here I have studied how internal activations can be used to understand behavioral changes before the outputs
* SC26 programme page: \[<https://sc26.conference-program.com/presentation/?id=pap693&sess=sess217]%28https://sc26.conference-program.com/presentation/?id=pap693&sess=sess217%29>; fast parallel k-clique counting I worked on creating the independent set counter; the key insight was to reformulate the clique counting problem as complementary independent set counting problem which attacks the representational space and gives large speedup by reading the search tree depth (1,356x on my step, 16,631x on 192 cores for the full team system)
* Previously Senior ML Engineer at Microsoft Azure OpenAI (owned GPT-4o and GPT-4o mini release validation and latency testing, cutting release evals from 3-4 days to 1), Senior ML Engineer at REAL Brokerage (agent verification layers and Temporal pre-merge gates), and Senior Data Scientist at IBM (built the 13-model code-generation eval standard).

### How much money have you raised in the last 12 months, and from where?

$100 for compute from a BlueDot Impact Rapid Grant in June 2026

title: IASER: Building Capacity for Safe, Ethical, and Responsible AI
creator: 5193af75-cf41-4630-838f-77559f9d02fd
description:
# IASER: Building Capacity for Safe, Ethical, and Responsible AI

## Project summary

We started IASER in July 2026 to bring Muslim researchers, scholars and technology professionals together to work on AI safety.

Since then, more than 100 people have joined. We've made progress on AI evaluations, developed tools such as Ansari, and started work on practical guidance and training.

The difficulty is keeping everything moving. Most of our members are volunteers with jobs and other commitments. We have research projects underway, but not enough people with dedicated time to coordinate them, follow up on work or maintain what we've built.

We're looking to raise $100,000–$500,000 over the next 12 months to address this. Our first priority is to support the people already doing the work, finish what we've started and build a stronger foundation for IASER.

## What are this project's goals? How will you achieve them?

We have no shortage of ideas or people interested in helping. What we lack is the capacity to organise the work properly.

Our first priority is project coordination. With more than 100 members, we need a better system for matching volunteers to tasks, making responsibilities clear and following projects through to completion. We also need to be more realistic about how many projects we can take on.

The second priority is our existing research.

JaleesBench and FaithfulBench examine how AI models answer religious questions and behave under pressure. JaleesWeights explores model post-training, while Ansari provides a free Islamic AI assistant.

We want to continue these projects, improve the evaluations and publish findings that others can check and build on. This requires computing resources, technical work, review and maintenance.

We're also developing an Islamic Ethics Guidebook for Tech Professionals. Many Muslims working in technology face questions about the systems they're helping build, particularly around surveillance, discrimination and other potential harms. We're gathering evidence of these challenges and working on guidance that addresses real situations. We're also collaborating with Yaqeen Institute on an Islamic Ethics Framework for AI.

Another area is education. Dr Waleed Kadous and collaborators have already developed and delivered practical AI workshops for imams. In a pilot survey of 84 imams, more than half reported using AI in their religious work, but fewer than half felt equipped to answer questions about it.

We want to improve the training and make it available more widely, with particular attention to misinformation, fabricated references and knowing when AI outputs need checking.

We don't expect to do everything at once. During the first two months, we'll review our projects, agree on priorities and assign responsibilities based on the funding available.

## How will you know it worked?

I'd consider the funding worthwhile if, a year from now, IASER is finishing more of the work it starts and is less dependent on a handful of volunteers.

We'll track completed projects, research publications, volunteer contributions and the use of our resources.

For our research, we'll report what we've tested and found, including results that don't support our expectations.

For the ethics guidebook and training, we'll ask the people using them whether the material addresses their actual needs and what should change.

We'll also review finances and project progress every quarter.

After six months, we'll decide which activities are worth continuing and which need to change. At the end of the year, we'll publish a report on what we've achieved, what hasn't worked and how the money was spent.

## How will this funding be used?

We're requesting between $100,000 and $500,000 for 12 months.

Most of the budget is for people. We need dedicated time for research, engineering, coordinating volunteers and keeping projects moving.

The remaining funding would cover research costs, maintaining tools such as Ansari, preparing educational resources, training and essential running expenses.

We will adjust the scope depending on how much we raise.

At $100,000, we'd concentrate on project coordination, essential services and a few priority projects.

At $250,000, we'd be able to support more research and community activities.

At $500,000, we could deliver the wider programme and bring in dedicated staff or contractors where needed.

These are estimates. We won't commit to spending until we've confirmed actual costs and responsibilities.

## Who is on your team? What's your track record on similar projects?

IASER is new, but our team brings experience from AI research, technology companies, education, Islamic scholarship and nonprofit organisations.

Our Steering Committee includes:

**Dr Waleed Kadous** has worked in AI for more than 25 years, including senior roles at Google, Uber and Canva. He developed Ansari and the AI for Imams course and has contributed to our model evaluation research.

**Dr Mohammed Ansari** is a senior applied scientist at Amazon with a PhD in Computer Sciences from the University of Wisconsin–Madison.

**Dr Agnes Chong** has worked in nonprofit leadership and philanthropy, including roles at the American Muslim Community Foundation and CAIR.

**Bara Elhag** brings experience in technology sales, business development and consulting.

**Abdus-Sami Hoda** works in education and technology leadership and is involved with Ummatics Institute and Mubeen Institute.

**Hassan Kazi** has a background in management consulting at Deloitte and Accenture and serves on the board of Justice For All Canada.

Our Islamic Advisory Board includes **Dr Mohamed AbuTaleb**, Vice President of Research at Yaqeen Institute, and **Shaykh Umer Khan**, a member of the Fiqh Council of North America and technology executive.

These are not full-time positions at IASER.

We also have work that people can examine today:

* [**JaleesBench**](https://arxiv.org/abs/2608.07508) **and** [**FaithfulBench**](https://arxiv.org/abs/2609.13634)**:** Published research evaluating AI responses to religious questions and behaviour under pressure.
* [**JaleesWeights**](https://github.com/iaser-ai/jaleesbench/tree/main/jaleesweights)**:** Post-training experiments with publicly available documentation and preliminary findings.
* [**Ansari**](https://askansari.ai/)**:** A free Islamic AI assistant with publicly [available code.](https://github.com/iaser-ai/ansari)
* [**Islamic Ethics Guidebook for Tech Professionals**](https://iaser.ai/projects)**:** Research and guidance currently being developed.
* [**AI for Imams:**](https://cluesmith.com/ai-for-imams) A six-hour practical workshop developed and delivered by Dr Waleed Kadous and Dr Hidayath Ansari.

We've also organised public discussions and presentations about AI and its implications for Muslim communities.

Some of this work began before IASER officially launched. We're now bringing these efforts together and trying to build an organisation that can support them properly.

More information about our team is available at [iaser.ai/about](https://iaser.ai/about).

## What are the most likely causes and outcomes if this project fails?

The biggest risk is spreading ourselves too thin.

A lot of our work depends on people contributing in their spare time. It's easy for a project to start with enthusiasm and then slow down when other commitments take priority.

Funding would give us more capacity, but we'd still need to make decisions about what to pursue. We could underestimate the cost of a project, struggle to find the right people or discover that something we've developed isn't particularly useful.

We plan to review projects regularly and be willing to stop work that isn't progressing.

If we don't raise enough money, we'll scale back rather than try to deliver the full programme.

If the wider plan doesn't succeed, the most likely outcome is that some research and community resources take longer to complete, and IASER remains dependent on volunteer time.

We'll report problems as they arise and account for how funding has been used.

## How much money have you raised in the last 12 months, and from where?

IASER only launched in July 2026, and we're still establishing our fundraising arrangements.

So far, much of our work has been carried out by volunteers and founding members, using their existing time and resources.

We're approaching potential donors and preparing funding proposals, but we're distinguishing these discussions from money actually committed.

We want this grant to help us move from relying almost entirely on voluntary contributions to having enough consistent support to deliver our projects and maintain them.

**Confirmed funding received from other sources:** IASER officially launched in July 2026, so we're still in the early stages of fundraising.

Most of what we've achieved so far has relied on volunteers and work developed by our founding team.

We've grown to over 100 members and are now approaching potential funders to help us support and expand this work.

We're developing funding proposals and donor relationships, but we won't count applications or informal discussions as money raised.

We'll update our fundraising figures as commitments are confirmed.

This campaign is an important step towards giving IASER the people and resources needed to move beyond volunteer-led work and become a more sustainable organisation.
