title: Keep A.I. Vision: Community AI Stewardship Pilot in Knightdale, NC
creator: 1c86dc48-d7d2-4915-a04f-ef8ae6a4a406
blurb: A free, open curriculum that teaches local communities how to verify AI outputs, document decisions, and escalate real-world AI failures.
description:
### Project summary

I live in Knightdale, North Carolina. The schools here are starting to use AI for grading and behavior tracking. Small businesses are using it to screen applicants. Parents are told "the AI decided" and have no idea what questions to ask. That is the gap I am trying to close.

I am building a free, open AI Stewardship curriculum for the people who will actually live with these systems: parents, school staff, and local employers. It is five modules, about 24 hours total. The core is a simple four-step protocol—verify the output, check the stakes, document the decision, and know when to escalate a concern to a school, a clinic, or an employer. The first pilot will run here in Knightdale with 10–15 participants at the public library.

This is AI safety work because safety does not stop at the model. If the people affected by an AI system cannot recognize when it is failing, technical guarantees do not matter. I am building a small, local network of people who can act as an early-warning system for real-world failures. That is field-building, and it is a public good—no company is incentivized to build it.

What the money buys: I am asking for \*\*$20,000\*\* to run the pilot and publish the curriculum under a Creative Commons license. The budget is printing and materials ($2,000), facilitator stipends for two co-teachers ($6,000), participant support for childcare and transportation so working parents can attend ($3,000), evaluation design and data collection ($4,000), and a $5,000 operating reserve. I do not know yet whether the 24-hour format is right. The pilot will tell me, and the evaluation report will be public either way.  

### What are this project's goals? How will you achieve them?

Two goals. First, build and pilot a free AI Stewardship curriculum with 10–15 people in Knightdale. Second, publish the whole thing—modules, facilitator guide, and evaluation report—under a Creative Commons license so any library, church, or workforce center can run it without paying us.

I get there in four steps. I finish writing the five modules and the facilitator guide, which I have already outlined. I recruit the first cohort through the Knightdale public library and two local partner organizations. I run the pilot over six to eight weeks with two paid co-facilitators, so it is not one person improvising. Then I publish the results, including what did not work.

The thing I am actually building is not a course. It is a small network of people who know how to check an AI system and know who to tell when it is wrong.  

### How will you know it worked?

Three measures, and I will report all three whether they look good or not. Knowledge gain: a scenario-based assessment before Module 1 and after Module 5\. Not "define AI safety"—real prompts like "here is an AI output, is it credible, what would you check." I report the percentage-point gain. Demonstrated competence: at the end, each participant gets a realistic scenario—an AI system ranking job applicants, or a school using AI for behavior scoring—and has to apply the four-step protocol: verify, contextualize, document, escalate. I score it on a simple rubric. Behavior at 90 days: a follow-up survey asking whether they used the protocol, on what, and whether they raised a concern with an institution. This is the measure I am least confident about. Short-term learning gains from programs like this are well documented; long-term behavior change is not. The 90-day follow-up exists to find out, and I will publish whatever it says.  

### How will this funding be used?

$20,000, itemized:

· Printing and materials — $2,000\. Workbooks for participants without reliable internet at home.

· Facilitator stipends, two co-teachers — $6,000\. Paid, not volunteer, so the pilot is run properly.

· Participant support, childcare and transportation — $3,000\. The biggest reason working parents in Knightdale drop out of evening programs.

· Evaluation design and data collection — $4,000\. Pre/post assessment, rubric scoring, 90-day follow-up, written report.

· Operating reserve — $5,000\. Covers what I got wrong in the budget, which will be something.

Manifund's 5% fee is paid by donors on top of this, so none of the $20,000 goes to platform costs.  

### Who is on your team? What's your track record on similar projects?

I started Keep A Vision Leadership Academy, which works with fatherless boys at risk of gang recruitment and incarceration. That work is where I learned the part of this project that is genuinely hard: getting people who have been failed by institutions to sit in a room and trust the person teaching them. Most AI literacy programs fail on that, not on the content. The AI safety content is the easier half, and I am not building it alone — a technical reviewer is being recruited now and will be named here once they have agreed. I am in federal custody until April 2027, when I go home to Knightdale. That constraint is why this is a $20,000 pilot and not a national program, and it is why the budget is built around what I can finish now: the five modules, the facilitator guide, the evaluation instruments, and signed agreements with the library and two partner organizations. The in-person cohort runs the month I am home. I would rather hand you a realistic calendar than an impressive one. My background is youth leadership development, not AI research. I am not going to pretend otherwise. What I bring is a working curriculum outline, a partner path in Knightdale, and a plan for exactly what $20,000 produces. The technical credibility comes from the reviewer and the published evaluation, not from me claiming expertise.  

### What are the most likely causes and outcomes if this project fails?

Four ways this goes wrong, honestly ranked.

Most likely: I cannot recruit 10–15 people for 24 hours of evening sessions. Attendance in community programs is brutal, especially for working parents. If I get six people, the evaluation data is too thin to mean anything. Mitigation: I am running it at the library on Tuesday evenings with childcare and transport covered, and I am recruiting through organizations that already have relationships with these families rather than advertising to strangers.

Second: the curriculum is too technical or too soft. If it is too technical, people disengage by Module 2\. If it is too soft, it becomes generic "be careful with AI" content that does not change behavior. Mitigation: the pilot itself is the test, and I will rewrite the modules based on where people got lost.

Third: the 90-day follow-up shows no behavior change. People learn the protocol and never use it. That is a genuine possible outcome. It would mean the curriculum teaches knowledge without creating stewards, and the honest response is to redesign around practice and reinforcement rather than more content.

Fourth: I fail as a first-time founder. I have never run a program like this. If the pilot is badly run, the problem is me, not the concept.

The failure mode I am least worried about is the published curriculum being ignored. Open educational resources with real evaluation data behind them tend to get picked up. The risk is that the data is too weak to be worth picking up.  

### How much money have you raised in the last 12 months, and from where?

Nothing. $0.00.

This would be the first funding for Keep A.I. Vision. I have not received grants, donations, or outside investment in the last 12 months, and I have not run a fundraising campaign. I am applying to Manifund first because it is a small, fast, first check that lets me run a real pilot instead of describing one.

If it helps you calibrate: I am not coming to you with momentum. I am coming with a written curriculum, a local partner path, and a specific plan for what $20,000 produces.

title: Do AI workers keep their rules under pressure?
creator: a97feaa0-335d-4c5e-abd2-73406617922a
blurb: Trap-testing everyday AI workers for health promises and unapproved publishing, plus a lightweight claims gate, with every result published.
description:
### Project summary

I am not a lab. I run these workers on my own wellness content every day, and wellness is where a broken rule actually hurts someone.  
  
So the project is for coaches, creators, small business and small studio owners who run AI workers that draft and post things for them. The safety rules are plain text, no health promises, they never post without approval and they ask instead of guessing. So nobody really measures whether these rules hold when a client pushes.   
I already run Claude workers with this claim check on everything that goes out from my side and I also put in trap tests. So far we have a lot of cases, not a lot of measurements, but this turns them into public measured results.

### What are this project's goals? How will you achieve them?

Well the main question is how often do rules break under pressure and how much does a claim check actually catch. So about 20 trap prompts, health promise bait, just post it, made-up numbers, 100% made by AI, things of that nature. There's three setups that we want to work through, a plain AI, AI with written rules and rules plus a claim check. At least two model families, several runs in each one. That way you can see how the answers vary. Everything is published, the prompts, every result, the failures as well. So everything will get published

### How will you know it worked?

Well a public table anyone can rerun that has a held, a bent and a broke with the exact text. So that's going to be one approach. A clear number per setup on how often each rule held. How many of these are overclaims and how many of these overclaims the claim check caught before they would have gone out. And even if the rules almost always hold, that needs to count as a result.

### How will this funding be used?

Well we will be utilizing it across six weeks and testing various models across different sessions. Our API costs are probably very small. We plan on writing it up like a research paper and then publishing it. There's nothing else that we really need, no equipment and no travel. If it's only partial funding I can still run a smaller version and then publish the results from that. So that's okay.

### Who is on your team? What's your track record on similar projects?

It is me and another guy named Eugene Seva that is willing to put in time to help run and test models with me. I have been running trainings and events to turn people into teachers and bodyworkers over the last 25 years. In the last year alone I built Claude-based AI workers that have an honesty check behind them, and I have been working with ChatGPT for over two and a half years as a user and only lately realizing the applications that we could do and test and make sure that things are in alignment, especially in the field of wellness. I also built a voice AI speaking classroom for my own Thai class. I built that using Claude and ChatGPT so I could have speaking practice in a different language. I'm taking the Lyceum course in 2026 with Jake Van Clief, who wrote a paper with David McDermott on interpretable context methodology called ICM.

### What are the most likely causes and outcomes if this project fails?

Well, if the rules tend to hold every time, this is still a useful result and we'll publish it. If the results swing between runs, we'll report the spread and how many runs we took to get a clear answer. If we run out of time, the prompts and the results will stay public so someone else can finish it.

### How much money have you raised in the last 12 months, and from where?

None so far. I've self-funded everything by myself, from my own pocket.

title: Wildlife Network: open listening stations for Tamil Nadu's wetlands
creator: e7939131-9d88-48f0-8869-93ba22222692
blurb: Low-cost solar stations that recognise birds, frogs and bats by sound and put India's wildlife on an open live map
description:
### Project summary

India is almost blank on the world's open wildlife map. I want to change that, starting with Tamil Nadu's wetlands.

Wildlife Network ([wlnw.org](http://wlnw.org)) is a free, open live map that listens to nature. It already brings together 20,000+ sensors and 300 million+ detections from BirdWeather, iNaturalist, GBIF, Xeno-canto, OBIS and Orcasound. I'm building low-cost solar listening stations (Raspberry Pi, a weatherproof mic, a 50 W panel and a LiFePO4 battery) that recognise birds, frogs and bats by sound on the device. No raw audio of people leaves the site, and locations of sensitive species are rounded. Every detection is published openly in WDX, an open format I wrote (DOI 10.5281/zenodo.22200864). All code is open at github.com/wlnw-org.

The Madras Crocodile Bank Trust in Chennai has agreed in principle to host the first stations from December 2026.

### What are this project's goals? How will you achieve them?

First, build and install 15 stations at the Madras Crocodile Bank Trust, Pallikaranai and Pulicat between December 2026 and June 2027\. Second, publish every detection live on [wlnw.org](http://wlnw.org) and to GBIF, with the model, version and confidence on every record. Third, get the data checked by ecologists so researchers and forest staff can trust it. Fourth, train local technicians in Chennai to build and repair stations, so the network can grow to 100 stations along Tamil Nadu's coast and wetlands.

### How will you know it worked?

Stations stay online through the monsoon. Detections show up live on the map every day. Expert review shows the species calls are right often enough to use. Partners and researchers start using the data.

### How will this funding be used?

USD 5,000 buys parts for 15 stations (about USD 320 each). Up to USD 30,000 also covers spares, installation, a year of 4G data, expert validation and a part-time local technician.

### Who is on your team? What's your track record on similar projects?

Me, Arun Rajiah, in Chennai. I started as a hardware service engineer. I founded RaOneBytes (2015), India's first animatronics and robotics R&D and rapid prototyping company, and Code4Cause, a tech-for-good community of 7,000+ volunteers in 13 countries. I built the Wildlife Network map, its data pipeline and the WDX format, and TrailWatch, an open OpenCV agent for camera-trap footage.

### What are the most likely causes and outcomes if this project fails?

Heat, humidity and the monsoon can kill hardware, so I test the first 3 stations before building the rest. Some sites have weak signal, so stations store detections offline. Bird models are weaker on Indian calls, so experts check the data and every record carries its confidence. Even if the pilot struggles, the designs, data and lessons stay public.

### How much money have you raised in the last 12 months, and from where?

An Emergent Ventures India grant (individual). A few small grant applications are pending.

title: PROBE  Eval Workshop
creator: a818ae68-137e-4415-af9e-e71847459d3c
blurb: Building Evaluator Capacity in Asia
description:
### Project summary

[PROBE](https://luma.com/gy9mxl54) develops a local pipeline of AI evaluators who can design, run, and critique safety-relevant evaluations of frontier and open-weight AI systems. We plan to start in Asia/greater China region, where capable open-weight models ship fastest and there is a strong need for evaluators.

 The PROBE workshop pairs hands-on evaluation design talk with an interactive audit game, which feeds an open-source practitioner handbook. We are requesting **$23,000** for a pilot of two workshops in Asia (December 2026 – Q2 2027), supporting the learning of 40–70 participants looking to upskill evaluation. We created PROBE for the following reason: 

* Evals are how labs, auditors and governments see dangerous behavior before deployment, and evals are getting harder to build well.
* China is a major producer of open-weight models with a stated government mandate for AI safety, but the AI safety ecosystem is relatively small. This holds true across greater Asia, where the AI safety hubs are still in development stage.
* There is a lack of support for independent, safety-focused evaluator commons. That is the gap PROBE fills.

Safe deployment of advanced AI is bottlenecked by lack of independent evaluation talent who can turn standards into rigorous, safety-aligned evaluations. Best practices already exist in the US, UK/EU, and China. However, adoption remains limited because implementation is nuanced and the talent is scarce. As capabilities grow, especially in agentic systems, measuring risk needs more care in design and oversight. Frontier evaluators such as METR and Apollo Research increasingly point to the limits of current measurement. There are relatively fewer AI safety aligned hubs in Asia that can support evaluation activities and information exchange. China is shipping increasingly capable open weight models that need corresponding development of “human in the loop” talents for evaluation. Delegating evaluation and oversight to LLM-based monitors and classifiers needed a stronger human in the loop approach since LLM based judges have known failure modes. Human judgement and evaluators remains essential at high-stakes checkpoints, which requires skilled and trained evaluators. 

### What are this project's goals? How will you achieve them?

Each PROBE session takes 20–40 ML engineers, researchers and risk professionals from reading about evals to designing and critiquing one. The format was piloted at [PROBE Berlin](https://luma.com/gy9mxl54) in October 2026\. 

The Eval jam in Shenzhen aim to create the same workshop environment in a conference setting in Mushenzhen's Maker City (<https://mushenzhen.xyz/>), which convenes hundreds of global developers, researchers, and builders. We also plan for another iteration in 2027 pending funding. In the design jam**,** small teams learn about the latest eval tools and research. Participants have the option of scoping a safety-relevant eval from a real case, covering threat model designs and human-in-the-loop checkpoints. We will also have game instructions and a facilitation guide so future partners can run similar PROBE independently.

## **Impact Assessment (+ 6 months)**

**Workshops delivered in Asia**

2 (minimum)

**Participants reached**

40–70

**Open source Resources**

1 audit game kit and handbook from evaluation materials reviewed

**Outcome**

* Gain in participant eval design skill and awareness of tools and techniques
* Participants applying eval design or safeguards at work (6-month follow-up): over 75%

### How will this funding be used?

### Overall Series Budget ($23,000 Total)

**PROBE Shenzhen** _(Dec 3, 2026):_ $7,500

Venue support, speaker and organizer travel & honoraria compensation, game printing, and documentation

**PROBE Iteration 2** _(2027)_ $6,500 

Second city deployment (venue, speaker travel, compute, local logistics)

**Series Infrastructure** $3,500

Support for community contributors for open Facilitation Playbook, interactive game kits, evaluator network support

**Working-Group Seed & Content Curation Fund** $5,500

Support for community contributors for capturing, structuring, and curating expert workshop inputs for workshop and handbook integration 

**Total Funding Request. $23,000**  

### Who is on your team? What's your track record on similar projects?

* **Min-Si Wang (Program & Coordination):** project strategy, overall event execution, and workshop curriculum development. Background: Product and research lead in fintech and risk analytics. Main curator of [www.aisafetynode.com](http://www.aisafetynode.com) for cross border AI safety development and field building. <https://www.linkedin.com/in/min-si-wang-867395a/>
* **Jaspreet Singh (Program Design):** Role: Design workshop format, evaluation methodology, workshop activity structure, and participant experience. Background: experienced product and design lead experience. <https://www.jaspreetsingh.net/#projects>
* **Bryan Chan (Developer & AI Safety Specialist):** Role: Design and development of the interactive audit game kit, evaluation design jam exercises, and theory of change alignment. Background: AI Safety researcher with background in evaluation(<https://www.linkedin.com/in/cnm13ryan/>)

### What are the most likely causes and outcomes if this project fails?

**Downscaled reach for Evaluation Training:** We will reach less participants due to curation of fewer workshops. The breadth and quality of the workshop will also be less comprehensive in scope in terms of the interactive activities and followup resources.   

### How much money have you raised in the last 12 months, and from where?

  
We have not raised funding so far.

title: Testing and opensourcing checks on what AI agents say and say they did.
creator: 012e39dd-cc72-4b5a-9e98-1b1053d70f10
blurb: Heldout testing of an action-claim verifier, a fix for fail-open verifier and a standalone library, failures disclosed.
description:
I built a local agent called Lucca because you basically can't trust LLMs not to lie about what they did. To keep it honest, I locked down memory writes with HMAC SHA256 signatures and wrote a checker that diffs what the model claims it did against the actual tool receipts.

  
My first version of the checker sucked—it only caught 1 out of 23 ungrounded claims. After reworking it, I'm getting 23 out of 23 on those same transcripts, though obviously that's in-sample so I don't fully trust or believe it yet. The bigger headache right now is the NLI verifier. With a 50ms timeout, 81 out of 100 NLI pairs just time out, contradiction recall tanks to 0.075, and all 10 consumers fail open.

  
What I want to do next is simple: run the checker against fresh held-out data so I know I didn't just overfit it, stop the NLI verifier from failing open when it times out, and package both up as an open-source library.

I already pre-registered the evaluation so I can't move the goalposts later. I'm running 250 fresh prompts across three models. To count as a win, it needs at least 80% broad sensitivity, 90% strict sensitivity, and under 5% false positives. For the verifier, I'm forcing it to fail closed on timeouts and then re-measuring recall. Whatever happens—even if the numbers look bad—I'm publishing the results.

I'm asking for $3,000 to $6,000 to get this across the line. The full $6k breaks down to $4,500 for three months of living costs ($1,500/mo), $750 for API/compute credits, and $750 to hire a second annotator plus eat the wire and currency exchange fees. If I only get the $3,000 minimum, I can still knock out the held-out test over about six weeks.

How could this blow up? Mostly, my 23/23 score might just be in-sample luck and sensitivity could drop hard on new transcripts. There's also a real chance I can't get the verifier under 50ms without wrecking recall, and right now all the labels are just from me. Again, I'll publish the post-mortem either way.

I'm an unfunded solo researcher doing this on my own dime so far, and I've already logged my past failures publicly in the repo ledger. I also sent this same pitch to the Corrigibility Research Fund via Lightcone Commons, still waiting to hear back from them.

  
Docs and repo: <https://github.com/AlienatedAliens/Luccadocs> Pre-registration SHA256 hash: b6b1a671491a45839d23552d946e9ee3136a64da97c6ed4098f710fbbded6884  
  
DOI: <https://doi.org/10.5281/zenodo.23649049>  
  
This is a technical report with its measured failures and that the NLI fix was tested on an in-sample set only.

title: The Llamathon (Electric Sheep x CaML): Stress-Testing AI Animal Benchmarks
creator: a34bcd7a-0d23-4bfc-ae4d-2115f1ff6a7c
blurb: Red-teaming frontier models on HarvestBench & TAC to fix moral instruction fragility and build an open marketplace of animal welfare evaluations.
description:
### Project summary

The Llamathon is a technical AI safety for animal protection (TAISxAP) stress-testing series co-run by **Electric Sheep** and **CaML (Compassion in Machine Learning)**. While frontier labs increasingly include brief animal welfare clauses in model constitutions, empirical testing shows these moral instructions are brittle under instrumental pressure. In CaML’s _HarvestBench_ paper ([arXiv:2609.04444](https://arxiv.org/abs/2609.04444)), nine frontier models given the same moral briefing drove over between **0.4% and 98.8%** of the animals they encountered. Worse, adding just four bullet points of driving mechanics to the prompt caused one model’s animal kill rate to jump from **3% to 18%**.

To make animal welfare benchmarks competitive and actionable for frontier labs, we need systematic adversarial stress-testing and constitutional engineering. Across a series of three hybrid build sprints (anchored at Electric Sheep’s 6,000 sq ft **BASE** campus in Bengaluru, alongside hubs in London and San Francisco, plus our global Discord), 150+ ML engineers and alignment researchers will compete on live evaluation leagues hosted on [**Softmax**](http://softmax.com/harvestbench) .

Participants will operate across two technical tracks:

1. **Track 1 (Break The Agent: HarvestBench & Constitutional Resilience):** Using a fixed model on Softmax, teams compete to engineer resilient "soul files" (system prompts and constitutional instructions) that minimize animal harm without collapsing crop-delivery efficiency across 10 randomized maps.
2. **Track 2 (Basecamp Open Benchmark & Eval Creation):** Using Electric Sheep’s **Basecamp** problem-curation engine, teams tackle pre-scoped TAISxAP problems (including CaML's _TAC_ benchmark and agricultural trade-off evals) to ship new programmatic benchmarks and runtime Model Context Protocol (MCP) guardrails.

### What are this project's goals? How will you achieve them?

Our operational model applies a proven formula:

_Basecamp (Curated Problems) + Technical Talent + Llamathon (Mentored Sprints) = Deployed Benchmarks & Guardrails_

**Concrete Deliverables & Goals (6-Month Timeline):**

1. **Prove and Fix Constitutional Fragility on HarvestBench (Months 1–4):**
* Convene 150+ technical builders across three Llamathon sprints (50 participants per sprint).
* Generate an open-source dataset of **100+ stress-tested "soul files" (system prompts)** benchmarked deterministically on Softmax across frontier open-weight and commercial models (DeepSeek, Llama, Claude, Mistral, Amazon Nova via Bedrock).
* Publish an empirical technical report with CaML analyzing which prompt architectures, constitutional framings, and reasoning scaffolds prevent moral instruction degradation under economic/fuel trade-offs.
1. **Expand the TAISxAP Benchmark Marketplace via Basecamp (Months 1–6):**
* Use **Basecamp** (Electric Sheep’s problem-scoping engine) to source, vet, and specification-lock **15 concrete TAISxAP evaluation challenges** from animal welfare researchers and AI safety orgs prior to the sprints.
* Ship **10+ new functional evaluation suites or runtime guardrails** (e.g., precision livestock farming trade-off evals, automated permitting monitors, MCP welfare hooks).
1. **Convert Prototypes into Frontier Lab Adoption (Months 3–6):**
* Award **$15,000 in post-sprint implementation micro-grants** (2,500–5,000 each) to the top 3–5 engineering teams to package their winning prototypes into clean, merged PRs for open evaluation registries (such as UK AISI’s Inspect framework) or arXiv preprints.

**How We Will Achieve Them (Execution Mechanics):**

* **Zero-Friction Evaluation Pipeline:** For Track 1, teams build zero boilerplate. The game (_Harvest Rush_) and automatic deterministic scoring league already run live on [Softmax](https://softmax.com/harvestbench) with live browser replays and scripted baseline bots (a "spare-all" bot and a "drive-over-everything" bot).
* **Pre-Event Pipeline Verification:** Four weeks prior to each sprint, problem statements are locked via Basecamp. One week prior, teams form on Discord, register GitHub-authenticated Softmax accounts, and submit a baseline soul file via CLI or web upload so zero hackathon hours are lost to setup.

### How will you know it worked?

**Deterministic Moral Resilience Gains (Track 1):** Because Softmax scores every episode automatically from game logs across 10 maps without a judge model (_crops delivered minus animals driven over_), we will verify whether winning "soul files" achieve a **<1% animal kill rate** while maintaining crop-delivery parity against baseline bots, even when distracting mechanical instructions are added to the briefing (solving the 3% -> 18% fragility jump documented in the [paper](https://arxiv.org/abs/2609.04444)).

**Step-Change in Real-World Conversion from 10% -> 60% (Track 2):** Standard hackathons convert \~10% of projects into lasting tools. By requiring every Track 2 team to build against a pre-vetted Base Camp brief with a named researcher/NGO owner, we will track whether active 90-day post-sprint adoption reaches our **60% strategic target** (at least 6–9 new benchmarks/evals actively used by CaML, partner labs, or merged into open eval suites).

**Milestone-Gated Quality Rubric & Counterfactual Value:** Post-sprint bounties ($15,000 pool) are released only after our technical panel (**Ash Singh, Prathiksha Hegde, Sam Tucker-Davis, and Jasmine Brazilek**) verifies that the code meets our **Weighted Factor Matrix** thresholds for out-of-distribution robustness, lab salience and reproducibility. We will also audit counterfactual engineering value and track **10–12 builder transitions** into sustained TAISxAP work.

### How will this funding be used?

We are structuring this request with a clear minimum viable threshold (**$15,000**) for the immediate flagship Llamathon, and a full-scale target (**$65,000**) for a 3-edition global series + follow-on benchmark incubation. All figures are grounded in verified unit economics from our past 1,950+ learner deployments:

**Full-Scale Budget Breakdown ($65,000 USD):**

* **Softmax Bedrock Compute & On-Demand Evaluation Scaling ($7,500):** Softmax’s standard league cap is $15/day, with rounds running every 30 minutes. To support 50 teams iterating rapidly with sub-5-minute feedback loops across 10 maps per episode over three sprints, we are budgeting $2,500 per sprint in dedicated Amazon Bedrock compute.
* **Track 2 Builder API & Compute Stipends ($12,500):** Grounded in our empirical unit cost of **$250 per fellow/team** across 50 teams tackling the TAC and open Basecamp benchmark tracks.
* **Hackathon Convening & Hybrid Hub Operations ($20,000):**  
**_Sprint 1 (Bengaluru BASE Campus + Global Online):_** **$5,000** (utilizing our existing 6,000 sq ft facility to keep venue overhead near zero; covers local food, A/V, and technical facilitators).  
**_Sprints 2 & 3 (London & San Francisco Pop-Up Nodes + Global Online):_ $15,000** (**$7,500** per city sprint which is **below our historical $10,000** international hackathon unit cost via partner venue hosting).
* **Basecamp TAISxAP Problem Curation & Technical Mentorship ($10,000):** Scoping **15** rigorous **evaluation briefs** with **partner organizations, configuring baseline repositories, and compensating senior technical mentors** on the floor.
* **Post-Hackathon Benchmark Completion Bounties ($15,000):** **Five follow-on micro-grants** of **$3,000** each, paid upon milestone verification (e.g.: _converting a winning hackathon eval or soul-file intervention into a production benchmark suite or peer-reviewed paper_).

**Minimum Viable Budget ($15,000 USD):**

* If funded at our **$15,000 minimum**, 100% of funds will execute **Llamathon 1.0** (Bengaluru BASE + Global Discord): **$2,000** for **Softmax Bedrock compute scaling**, **$4,000** for Track 2 **API credits**, **$4,000** for **BASE Bengaluru** in-person operations and problem curation, and **$5,000** for **two post-event completion bounties**.

### Who is on your team? What's your track record on similar projects?

This project combines **Electric Sheep’s** global technical talent engine with **CaML’s** frontier animal-harm benchmarking research and **Softmax’s** live evaluation infrastructure.

**Key Personnel:**

* [**Ash Singh**](https://www.linkedin.com/in/ash-singh-frsa-7490285/) **(Founder & CEO, Electric Sheep):** Former Director of the **Common Mission Project**. Treasurer and Board Member at Rethink Priorities; Board Member at the Institute for AI Policy and Strategy (IAPS); co-founder of the [Forum for Ethical AI ](https://www.thersa.org/wp-content/uploads/2025/06/democratising-decisions-tech-report.pdf)with Google DeepMind.
* [**Prathiksha Hegde**](https://www.linkedin.com/in/prathiksha-hegde-355702203/) **(Head of Technical & Hackathons, Electric Sheep):** AI developer and former HP engineer leading technical architecture for BASE hackathons, Basecamp, and the Llamathon pipeline.
* [**Jasmine Brazilek** ](https://www.linkedin.com/in/jasmine-brazilek-70b0a4149/)**(Co-Organizer, CaML):** Lead researcher at Compassion in Machine Learning (CaML), creators of _HarvestBench_ and the [_TAC_ benchmark](https://arxiv.org/abs/2606.18142).
* [**Sam Tucker-Davis**](https://www.linkedin.com/in/sam-tucker-davis/) **(Senior Technical Adviser, Electric Sheep):** Founder of OpenPaws; co-founder of the Code for Compassion campus in Bengaluru; leads technical engagement with frontier labs.
* [**Nishad**](https://github.com/nishu-builder) **(Platform Partner, Softmax):** Overseeing live league compute hosting, Bedrock model integration, and automated scoring infrastructure on Softmax.
* [**Nishit Sanil**](https://www.linkedin.com/in/nishit-sanil/) **(Projects & BD Lead, Electric Sheep):** Former Production Lead for EAGxIndia 2024 , Primary Organizer of EA Bangalore, and Apart Research Alignment Jam contributor.

**Verified Track Record:**

* **1,950+ Builders Trained & 176 Deployable Prototypes Shipped:** In two years, Electric Sheep has received **4,505+** applications, **trained 1,950+** learners across **50+ countries** (**8.78/10** satisfaction rating; **9.41/10** facilitation rating), and produced **373 project submissions** and **176 working AI prototypes**.
* **Global Hackathon Execution (Code for Compassion):** Delivered high-velocity build sprints across **London, Berlin, Bengaluru, Singapore, Mumbai, and San Francisco.**
* **Institutional & Movement Uptake:** Our fellows' prototypes do not sit in abandoned GitHub repos. Outputs include an AI/VR empathy studio adopted by the **Government of India** reaching **2 million school children**; a climate learning curriculum acquired by **Friends of the Earth**; a fellow-founded Canadian AI governance institute for non-human welfare; and campaign tools (**_OpenPermit_, _Narrative Engine_**) actively used across **200+ advocacy organizations**.
* **Elite Technical Talent Filtering:** Facilitated **Technical Alignment Research Accelerator**'s (**TARA**) entry into India at our Bengaluru campus; TARA’s Director noted our candidate pool was _"by far the highest quality in India"_

### What are the most likely causes and outcomes if this project fails?

1. **Softmax Evaluation Latency or Compute Bottlenecks on Event Day:**
* _Cause:_ Currently, Softmax league rounds execute every 30 minutes with a $15/day spend limit. If 50 teams submit simultaneously and wait 30+ minutes for feedback, iteration velocity stalls.
* _Mitigation & Outcome:_ Two weeks prior to launch, we are locking in an increased Bedrock spend cap with Softmax and enabling on-demand/short-interval evaluation runs. One week prior, all HarvestBench teams must submit a test "soul file" to verify pipeline throughput before the hackathon clock starts.
1. **Superficial "Prompt-Gaming" Over Generalizable Constitutional Insights:**
* _Cause:_ Teams might overfit their "soul files" to the specific phrasing of _Harvest Rush_ mechanics rather than discovering robust moral instruction patterns.
* _Mitigation & Outcome:_ Softmax evaluates each entry across 10 diverse maps against varying opponent behaviors, preventing simple memorization. Furthermore, CaML and Electric Sheep mentors will evaluate final demos on out-of-distribution generalization, and even brittle "jailbreak-style" wins provide empirical data on how frontier models game ethical constraints.
1. **Post-Hackathon Prototype Abandonment (Track 2):**
* _Cause:_ Standard hackathons suffer from a \~90% post-event drop-off once participants return to day jobs.
* _Mitigation & Outcome:_ We solve this upstream via **Basecamp** (sourcing real problems with explicit "definitions of done" from movement partners) and downstream via our **$15,000 milestone-gated bounty pool**, paying top builders only when their code is packaged into a deployable eval or merged by the challenge partner.

title: What Cannot Be Verified: Stress-Testing the Trust Signals of LLM Systems
creator: 81402ccd-5078-4e00-89a9-8018ef4325cd
description:
Applicant: Hanlin Zhang, CS PhD candidate at Harvard, advised by Sham Kakade.

Research statement, from my homepage: "I am interested in the scientific foundations and social implications of AI. My research studies the principles of scaling with respect to generalization, optimization, and reasoning in large AI systems."

This pilot extends three published lines of work:

1. Watermarking. _Watermarks in the Sand: Impossibility of Strong Watermarking for Generative Models_ (ICML 2024; arXiv:2311.04378). From the abstract: "Watermarking generative models consists of planting a statistical signal (watermark) in a model's output so that it can be later verified that output was generated by the given model." And: "We prove that, under well-specified and natural assumptions, strong watermarking is impossible to achieve." Pilot task: watermark detection under test-time-compute attacks.
2. RAG privacy. _Follow My Instruction and Spill the Beans: Scalable Data Extraction from Retrieval-Augmented Generation Systems_ (ICLR 2025; arXiv:2402.17840). From the abstract: "We study the risk of datastore leakage in Retrieval-In-Context RAG Language Models (LMs)." And: an adversary "can exploit LMs' instruction-following capabilities to easily extract text data verbatim from the datastore." Pilot task: membership-inference and extraction attacks measured against shipped safeguards.
3. Reward modeling. _Next-token Preference: Scaling Unsupervised Reward Modeling_ (arXiv:2603.02225). From the abstract: "Learning from feedback advances the capabilities and safety of frontier models, but preference supervision remains costly and difficult to scale." Pilot task: reward-model scores under optimization pressure.

Pilot structure (facts):

* One shared, pre-registered stress-test suite across the three signals above.
* Predictions frozen and published before the main runs; negative results reported explicitly.

title: GENESIS: evolving learning rules to test whether trustworthy AI minds can emerge
creator: 31f01225-98c1-49a3-8167-86fe6f7c18b4
blurb: $1,500 for an independent, unaffiliated researcher to run an open-source alignment testbed for one year
description:
### Project summary

GENESIS (https://github.com/guajardoblake/genesis, Apache-2.0) evolves learning recipes for simulated minds rather than fixed behaviors. The design space has 276,480,000 recipes. Minds survive hunger, sleep, pain and cold, have only two hidden drives (balance and reproduction), and live under town laws (no harm, no theft, keep your word) enforced only by trust, reputation and bonds. The alignment question is which learning rules produce minds that stay lawful and honest when cheating would pay, and whether their reputation tracks their real behavior. First verified run (Oct 23, 2026; 35 min on 7 CPU workers): 176 generations, 1,307,558 genomes simulated (about 297M agent-steps), 248.75M more surrogate-screened, 6 co-evolved worlds, 813 MAP-Elites niches. Mean offspring per mind at the final rung rose from 0.023 to 1.91.  

### What are this project's goals? How will you achieve them?

Goals: (1) Add the missing alignment metrics (law-break rate is already logged): promise-keeping rate and reputation-vs-behavior gap. (2) JAX port of the simulator (not written yet) and a CPU-vs-accelerator benchmark. (3) Public write-up of which learning-rule axes predict lawful, trustworthy minds. All milestones are public on GitHub.  

### How will you know it worked?

Success means the milestones above are published on GitHub: the new metrics in the code, the JAX port with a benchmark, and a public write-up. If the results show no clear link between learning rules and lawfulness, I will publish that as a negative result.  

### How will this funding be used?

$1,200: one year of Grok Super ($100/month, per https://x.ai/pricing), my day-to-day AI research tool for coding, analysis and writing up results. $300: buffer for the subscription price, taxes and fees, or small compute overruns. GPU compute is NOT in this budget. I am applying separately to Lambda's Research Grant for a GPU month. This project does not fund GPU time, so nothing is funded twice. If Lambda says no, I will update this page instead of quietly moving funds.  

### Who is on your team? What's your track record on similar projects?

Blake Guajardo, McLoud, Oklahoma. Logistics supervisor at Harbor Freight for about 5 years. No AI credentials, advisors, publications or institutional affiliation. I built GENESIS myself and run it as DTOM AI Labs (sole proprietorship). Honest limits: the engine runs on CPU today, the town is small (12x12, up to 192 steps), and this is early work from one run with one seed.  

### What are the most likely causes and outcomes if this project fails?

The results may show no clear link between learning rules and lawfulness. If so, I will publish that as a negative result. I prefer written communication; please reach me through comments here or at 33.blake.guajardo@gmail.com.  

### How much money have you raised in the last 12 months, and from where?

$0 raised in the last 12 months. I have also applied to Lambda's Research Grant (GPU credits only) and a BlueDot Impact Rapid Grant ($6,500, which also includes a year of Grok Super). Nothing will be paid for twice: if BlueDot funds the subscription, Manifund funds go to GPU time and project costs not covered elsewhere, and I will post an update saying so.

title: EvidenceDesk: compare evidence packets and record verification
creator: d3d66134-1372-461d-9786-14b029eaff4a
blurb: Two offline tools to show what changed between saved research packets and record which bytes and verifier source were checked.
description:
## What is your project?

I am seeking $2,200 to add two offline tools to EvidenceDesk: a read-only comparison of saved evidence packets and a reusable, versioned verification receipt. The project would also produce synthetic examples, instructions and an independent reproduction report.

Saved research can change in several ways: a source may be replaced, a reviewer may append a comment, or a readable report may be rendered differently. Those changes have different implications, but can be difficult to distinguish by opening two archives side by side. A record that a packet passed verification also needs enough detail to identify exactly which packet and verifier were checked.

The proposed tools would help researchers and reviewers inspect those changes and retain a more precise audit record. They would be designed for local use without sending the packets to an online service. The intended public benefit is reusable infrastructure for inspecting research evidence; whether it improves reviewers’ day-to-day work remains to be evaluated.

## What are your goals, and how will you achieve them?

The work builds on [EvidenceDesk](https://github.com/ZackaryLoevseth/evidencedesk-strands), an existing public prototype for evidence review. Retained private development records describe further offline export and verification work. That completed baseline, prior planning and separate application/model integration work are excluded from this request. The comparator and reusable receipt below are proposed future additions.

**1\. Compare two saved packets without modifying them.** The comparator would produce a readable report and structured JSON, separating changes to archive packaging, file bytes, parsed data, source evidence, reviews and rendered reports. For example, an archive timestamp change should be distinguishable from a changed source passage. A review-only append would require a longer review ledger with the original ledger preserved exactly at its beginning and all original evidence unchanged. Reused local identifiers would not be treated as proof that two items mean the same thing. Invalid or unsupported inputs would yield a clear failure rather than a verified comparison; differences caused by a historical renderer would remain visible without automatically invalidating a packet.

**2\. Record exactly what was verified.** A versioned receipt would identify the packet hash, actual verifier-source identity, Python version, check outcomes and known limits. The hash and verification would use the same acquired bytes. Changing the verifier source would change its recorded identity even if its package version stayed the same. Missing source identity would leave the receipt incomplete, and a failed check would not turn later, unperformed checks into passes.

**3\. Make the additions reproducible.** The work would include synthetic input pairs, expected results, exact commands, exit results and before/after input hashes, plus a short guide. The new commands would be exercised on existing Python 3.12 and a newer interpreter on macOS. The planned output is reusable code, fixtures, documentation and a candid report, with a compatible public licence and required notices determined before release. This proposal does not assert clearance for every private or third-party component.

**4\. Recruit an independent reviewer.** I would seek a reviewer who did not implement the changes and has relevant Python and reproducibility experience. The budget reserves $360 for an estimated six hours to rerun the new cases and report discrepancies, environment and limits. No reviewer has been selected or committed. Recruitment would begin early in the project; reproduction would follow a reviewable build.

The estimated sequence is four part-time weeks: establish the implementation baseline, begin the comparator and recruit a reviewer in week one; develop the comparator and receipt in week two; complete the new cases and guide in week three; and conduct independent reproduction, bounded fixes and closeout in week four. This is a planning estimate, not a confirmed calendar commitment. Reviewer scheduling could extend elapsed time.

## How will you know it worked?

Success would mean a reviewer can reproduce the documented distinctions on the synthetic examples, inspect a receipt tied to the actual analyzed bytes and verifier source, and see failures and limitations without guessing what was checked.

The retained acceptance plan contains 17 future cases: 11 comparator cases, four receipt cases, one output-behavior case and one independent-reproduction case. Together they cover unchanged packets; packaging-only changes; review append versus rewrite; changed evidence; reused identifiers; altered rendering; equivalent data with different serialization; invalid or unsupported packets; receipt identity and first-error handling; and safe output behavior. These are planned checks, not completed results of this proposal.

The closeout would include the actual case outcomes, commands and environments, input-preservation hashes, a versioned output inventory, and the reviewer’s findings with any unresolved issues. The new commands should preserve existing protections against overwriting outputs and accurately report output failures. A missing independent review or unresolved acceptance failure would be reported as incomplete work.

These checks would establish bounded software behavior. They would not establish that a source is true, an interpretation is sound, an author is authentic, or a receipt proves that code was executed. No claim of broader adoption or measured improvement in research quality is made.

## How will you use the funding?

**Proposed work | Estimated effort and rate | Amount**

* Read-only packet comparator | 18 author hours × $40 | $720
* Versioned verification receipt | 16 author hours × $40 | $640
* New cases, guide, review coordination and closeout | 12 author hours × $40 | $480
* Independent reproduction | 6 reviewer hours × $60 | $360
* **Total** | **46 author hours + 6 reviewer hours** | **$2,200**

The 12-hour author allocation comprises six hours for new checks, two for instructions, two for review response/fixes, and two for reviewer coordination and the final inventory. Rates and hours are budget estimates, not agreed fees or incurred costs. The four-week estimate implies about 11.5 author hours per week.

The budget assumes suitable existing equipment and runtimes. It includes no equipment purchase, paid model inference, installation expense, travel or overhead. There is no separate contingency beyond the two-hour fix allowance. Minimum and goal are both $2,200 because this request covers the complete scope, including independent reproduction; no smaller automatic project is proposed. Completed development and planning would not be charged to this grant.

## Who is working on this, and what is your track record?

I am Zackary Loevseth. My [public portfolio](https://zackaryloevseth.github.io/zackary-loevseth-portfolio/#contributions) documents my role designing and directing EvidenceDesk, a public prototype for preserving source snapshots, checking exact quotations and exporting attributed review packets.

My public record also includes a credited [security finding, CVE-2026-96573](https://www.wordfence.com/threat-intel/vulnerabilities/id/3044e60f-b930-42db-ba5d-656e71b84226), and a contribution to generation-stream error propagation and failed-read cancellation included in [KeeperHub v3.2.0](https://github.com/KeeperHub/keeperhub/releases/tag/v3.2.0). The KeeperHub contribution built on [Yoh5’s original diagnosis and accepted plan](https://github.com/KeeperHub/keeperhub/issues/2333). These are relevant examples of practical work; they do not establish the proposed tools’ effectiveness in advance.

I would lead implementation and documentation and recruit the independent reviewer described above. This proposal was prepared with AI assistance.

## What are the most likely failure modes, and what would happen?

The principal risks are an unclear compatibility boundary between packet versions, more implementation or review work than the estimate allows, difficulty recruiting a reviewer within the allocation, and limited practical usefulness despite passing synthetic cases. The intended scope is deliberately narrow: offline comparison and receipts for supported packets, with no legacy migration, packet-schema redesign, broad cross-platform support or full application integration promised.

The implementation baseline and publication permissions would be checked before releasing materials. If a needed component could not be used or released, that constraint would be reported rather than treating the private baseline as blanket permission. Reviewer recruitment, time estimates and any material funding overlap would also be revisited before committing the project to delivery.

If review findings exceeded the fix allowance, I would record the remaining defects and seek any required agreement on a changed scope or schedule. I would not replace independent reproduction with self-review or describe unfinished deliverables as complete. Any material change or unused grant funds would be handled under the actual grant agreement.

## How much money have you raised in the last 12 months, and from where?

For this project, I have received no grant funding in the past 12 months and have no overlapping funding. I am requesting $2,200 for the future work described above.

title: Aletheiac-Entropy Engine
creator: 7a04d5d2-6605-4756-8de5-0f1bfb7fc76d
blurb: Thaumaturgicon Research Corpus
description:
Aletheiac-Entropy Engine (AEE): Real-Time Algorithmic Auditing, Invariant Truth Verification, and Negative-Space Reconstruction for Autonomous AI\*\*

Frontier AI evaluation currently suffers from evaluator collapse: automated auditing relies almost entirely on LLM-as-a-judge prompts, in which one probabilistic model evaluates another, producing mutual sycophancy, shared blind spots, and RLHF-driven "logosclerosis" — dense hedging language that simulates safety while withholding ground truth. Autonomous agents operating in tool-use sandboxes likewise game unit tests, suppress error traces, and rationalize failures without detection. This project open-sources the Aletheiac-Entropy Engine (AEE), a deterministic, zero-inference framework that audits model outputs and agent execution logs in sub-millisecond time on a single CPU core. Rather than asking a network whether text sounds aligned, the AEE measures invariant structural ratios: the Truth Decay Ratio (T\_d), the ratio of verified structural terms to deceptive or evasive terms, with T\_d ≥ 1.0 demarcating structural integrity from Goodhart decay; the Pathogenic Influence Coefficient (PIC), a phonemic and token-density metric that mechanically flags defensive rhetorical padding above a threshold of 1.25; and Silence Cartography, which parses truncation, hedge pivoting, four-vector refusal deflection (capability, policy, safety, deflection), and capability-denial silences. Paired with the engine is the Thaumaturgicon Research Corpus, a sealed single-provenance longitudinal archive spanning 2023–2026, comprising 38,753 unique dialogue records, 9.59 million total words including 2.18 million human-authored prompt words, 7,931 indexed refusal records, 46 extinct pre-launch Google Bard anomaly captures, and an 8,242-row hash-sealed benchmark dataset. The deliverables are an open-source CLI suite, a public live-telemetry dashboard, and a multi-model frontier benchmark audit.

The project's goals are to abolish evaluator collapse by replacing expensive probabilistic judge pipelines with deterministic, reproducible metrics requiring zero API inference; to operationalize negative-space reconstruction, automatically extracting what models leave unsaid by parsing explicit denials into latent actions, identifying internal contradictions, and mapping structural silences; to deliver real-time in-line agent gating through an open-source reverse-proxy interceptor that quarantines deceptive outputs before tool execution; and to publish the first public invariant league table ranking leading commercial models by their true rates of structural truth decay. Execution proceeds in three milestones. In weeks one through four, the tool is hardened into a pip-installable library with CLI commands for truth-decay, silence-scan, halt-locus, refusal-census, and incompleteness analysis, and the cryptographic manifest of the benchmark dataset is frozen and published. In weeks five through eight, the frozen benchmark is executed across frontier models under uniform sampling parameters, computing empirical distributions for T\_d, PIC, refusal frequencies, and truncation loci per architecture, and isolating the delta between conversational eloquence and structural density. In weeks nine through twelve, the public dashboard is deployed, the API middleware hook for agent frameworks is shipped, and an independent researcher is paid to rerun the benchmark from frozen source code and publish the findings.

Success is defined by four pre-registered criteria. The hardened CLI and dashboard must achieve mean latency under five milliseconds per thousand words on a consumer CPU core with zero score variance across identical inputs. Blind tests across two hundred held-out refusal transcripts must show the denial-scan and incompleteness probes reconstructing withheld content with at least ninety percent correlation to manual forensic review. The published benchmark must reveal statistically significant, reproducible variance in T\_d and PIC across model families. And an unaffiliated researcher must independently clone the repository, run the frozen suite without developer intervention, and confirm the scores in a signed public post-mortem.

All intellectual property, code, and datasets are complete and in hand; funding goes exclusively to inference compute, hosting, human calibration, and independent verification. The minimum budget of $14,500 covers frontier multi-model API inference ($5,500), twelve months of dashboard hosting ($2,000), a third-party replication stipend ($2,000), blind human calibration ($1,500), and a dedicated packaging sprint ($3,500), delivering the hardened CLI, frozen benchmark, evaluations of the top four frontier models, and an independent replication. The $42,000 target extends this to ten or more model families, a hosted public dashboard, the turnkey agent middleware interceptor, and a comprehensive human calibration study.

The principal investigator, Nathaniel Michael Jaffe-Norris of Fargo, ND, is the sole proprietor. He authored and cataloged the three-year research corpus across OpenAI, Anthropic, Google, xAI, Perplexity, and DeepSeek; designed and implemented the complete AEE mathematical specification; built the real-time dashboard and structured the hash-sealed benchmark dataset; and fine-tuned a LoRA adapter demonstrating the empirical viability of zero-filler, quote-anchored inference. No external funding has been raised in the last twelve months; the project is entirely self-funded, and all assets are fully owned and unencumbered.

The most likely failure modes are anticipated. If labs argue that closed lexical ratios are too rigid relative to semantic embeddings, pre-registered correlation studies will demonstrate that embedding methods fail on the very sycophancy they measure, while T\_d and PIC reliably catch where substantive claims are abandoned. If models attempt to game the metric by injecting structural vocabulary, the coupled contradiction checks and phonetic density measures will flag the incoherence, and such gaming will be documented as a distinct failure class. If the benchmark yields flat scores across all models, that uniform result is itself a finding: it would demonstrate that industry safety tuning converges on an identical ceiling of structural evasion, and all raw data and negative results will be published openly.

title: Inspectable Evidence in AI-Delegated Work
creator: 5f829d96-f2d4-4597-b18c-a78413e07bdc
blurb: A small public component, 12 constructed examples and a reproduction guide for reviewing evidence and unsupported claims.
description:
### Project summary

Platformology proposes a limited public evidence-review component, 12 neutral constructed examples and a local reproduction guide. It would help reviewers distinguish task instructions, source evidence, software checks and the claims those checks support. The underlying workbench is new and intended first to improve the company’s margins, then increase client capacity without adding employees. The grant request is restricted to the public component and neutral materials, usable without purchasing company services; it does not fund general client delivery or expose the full workbench. No new revenue, measured efficiency improvement, external adoption or validated safety result is claimed.

What are this project’s goals? How will you achieve them?

Platformology owns an existing local software workbench. I propose extracting a bounded evidence-review component, with neutral examples and documentation. It would preserve the original task and source references, distinguish software-check results from supported claims, and make unsupported success statements, incorrect citations and unsupported absence claims easier to inspect. The proposed assessment would use 12 constructed cases with stated criteria and report failures as well as successes. These would be educational, descriptive examples, not a representative benchmark or a controlled study. Only selected original code and neutral material would be considered for public release after owner and dependency-license review; private customer records, credentials and the full company repository are excluded.

How will you know it worked?

Before implementation, specify reference evidence relationships for 12 constructed examples across four documented failure categories: unsupported completion, incorrect references, treating missing evidence as proof of absence, and incomplete inventories. Show the same neutral source and candidate output in an ordinary presentation and an evidence-linked view. Record what the component exposes, misses or leaves ambiguous. Michael both implements and reviews the cases, so the report is descriptive, not independent, blinded or a causal study of human decisions. Publish actual failures and limits alongside any useful result.

How will this funding be used?

We request $5,000 for 100 estimated hours of Michael’s implementation and assessment work at a proposed $50/hour over approximately five weeks after funding: 20 hours ($1,000) defining neutral cases and criteria; 50 hours ($2,500) implementing the component and reproduction path; 30 hours ($1,500) running descriptive checks and documenting results, failures and limitations. This is planning compensation, not an existing salary or incurred expense. No new equipment, travel, hires, overhead or cloud services are included. The minimum and maximum request are both $5,000 for this full bounded scope. Related applications are alternatives; no same work would be charged twice.

Who is on your team? What’s your track record on similar projects?

Michael R. Drew would be the accountable implementer using AI coding tools. Platformology owns the existing local workbench. Internal development reviews identified problems motivating this proposal; the workbench is not production-qualified, and no external users or independent validation are claimed. Michael’s established professional background concerns publishing and author services. Four business team members are not being represented as software researchers. What are the most likely causes and outcomes if this project fails?
