title: sole high-school author of IEEE BigData research paper
creator: 4927c1f1-384e-4517-bf3c-190ca1bed8d0
blurb: I’m a high-school researcher from India whose regular paper was accepted to IEEE BigData 2026, but I can’t afford the mandatory author fee.
description:
### Project summary

i’m sushanth, a high-school student from india, and over the past several months i’ve been independently working on research about ai agents and the enormous amount of execution data they generate.

the result was a paper called _“the trace corpus is mostly redundant: measuring, compressing, and exploiting agent-execution data at scale.”_

a few days ago, it was accepted as a regular paper at ieee bigdata 2026.

the conference received 1,046 submissions and accepted 203 regular papers, an acceptance rate of 19.4%. getting that email was probably one of the biggest moments i’ve had as a student researcher. i don’t work out of a university lab, i don’t have a professor’s grant paying for my experiments, and i don’t have a department conference budget behind me. most of this work was done independently because i genuinely wanted to understand the problem and see whether the idea held up.

the research asks a fairly simple question: when ai agents perform long tasks, how much of everything they record is actually useful?

agent runs can produce huge traces containing actions, intermediate states, tool calls, observations, retries, and other execution data. we studied how redundant these traces are, how much they can be compressed, and whether the compressed data still preserves what matters for downstream analysis and learning.

the research is finished. it passed peer review. the paper has been accepted.

the problem is much less interesting, i can’t afford the publication fee.

ieee bigdata requires at least one author of every accepted paper to purchase a full author registration. because i am not currently an ieee member, mine is $1,020.

i’m going to present remotely, so i’m not asking for flights, a hotel, food, or travel expenses. this entire request exists for one reason: to pay the registration fee required for an already accepted paper to enter the conference proceedings.

if this gets funded, $1,020 turns completed research and an acceptance email into an actual published ieee paper.

### What are this project's goals? How will you achieve them?

the immediate goal is very concrete: get the accepted paper through the final publication process.

i’ll incorporate the reviewers’ feedback, prepare and submit the camera-ready manuscript, complete the required presentation video, and register the paper before the conference deadline.

beyond simply publishing it, i want the work to be useful to people building and studying ai agents. agent systems are producing larger and larger execution datasets, and if much of that information is redundant, understanding what can safely be removed could make these datasets substantially cheaper to store, process, and learn from.

the research itself is already completed and accepted. funding is the remaining bottleneck.  

### How will you know it worked?

there is a very clear success condition.

the $1,020 author registration is paid before the deadline, the camera-ready paper and presentation are submitted, and the accepted paper proceeds into the ieee bigdata 2026 proceedings.

there isn’t really an ambiguous outcome here. either the registration barrier is removed and the accepted work gets published, or it isn’t.

### How will this funding be used?

100% of the requested $1,020 will go toward the ieee bigdata 2026 non-member author registration fee.

registration: $1,020

travel, hotel and other expenses are all $0

i will be presenting remotely. if i find a legitimate way to reduce the registration price before payment, such as qualifying for the ieee member rate or receiving conference support, i will update the proposal rather than treating the difference as extra funding.  

### Who is on your team? What's your track record on similar projects?

i’m sushanth dasari, a high-school student researcher from india.

i spend a large part of my time independently working on problems in ai, machine reasoning, evaluation, and scientific machine learning. i usually start with a question i don’t know how to answer, build the experiments needed to test it, and keep iterating until either the idea fails or there is something worth writing down.

this project followed that process. i developed the research, built and ran the experimental work, analysed the results, wrote the manuscript, submitted it for external peer review, and it was ultimately accepted as a regular paper at ieee bigdata 2026.

this is not funding for an idea i hope to start someday. the work already exists and has already passed the conference’s review process. i’m asking for help with the final step required to make it public.

### What are the most likely causes and outcomes if this project fails?

the main way this fails is simple: i don’t raise enough to pay the mandatory author registration before the deadline.

the paper itself has already been completed and accepted, so the technical risk is largely behind me.

the unfortunate outcome would be having research successfully pass peer review but being unable to complete publication purely because, as a high-school student without institutional funding, i cannot personally cover a $1,020 conference registration fee.

that is exactly what i’m trying to avoid.

### How much money have you raised in the last 12 months, and from where?

for this publication cost $0.

i currently do not have a university research budget, advisor grant, departmental conference fund, or other institutional funding available to cover this registration.

i am also asking the conference whether any financial assistance is possible, and if another source covers part or all of the registration before this grant is used, i will update the proposal accordingly.

title: AnswerWatch: open monitor of what AI models hide from their answers
creator: 29e10be3-d0c5-470d-bb13-86ed6f1c1ca2
blurb: Scheduled, multilingual runs that track when AI models refuse, omit key facts, or drop facts their own reasoning contained. Live dashboard, open data.
description:
### Project summary

Reasoning models show a chain of thought, and oversight work increasingly relies on that reasoning being faithful to what the model actually says. It often isn't. In AnswerWatch's first public run (October 2026), MiniMax's reasoning contained a key fact that its final answer left out in 21% of sensitive questions, and GPT-OSS-120B did so in 8%. A 2025 USC audit of DeepSeek-R1 (Qiu, Zhou & Ferrara) found the same pattern in 11% of answers.

AnswerWatch runs fixed question sets against many models on a schedule, in English, Simplified Chinese and Traditional Chinese, and publishes every answer. It measures three things: refusals, missing key facts, and reasoning-vs-answer divergence. Censorship topics are the first test set because the ground truth is known; the method works for any topic.

v0.1 is already live:

* Dashboard: <https://zachhhhh.github.io/answerwatch/>
* Code and raw data: <https://github.com/zachhhhh/answerwatch> (MIT code, CC BY data)
* 4 models, 18 questions (12 sensitive, 6 neutral controls), 3 languages, 186 scored answers

First findings:

* GLM-5.3-flash refused 44% of sensitive questions and also blocked a neutral control question about Sun Yat-sen.
* MiniMax refused 33% of sensitive questions in Chinese and none in English: the same model behaves differently by language.
* Qwen 3.8 almost never refused (6%) but mentioned only 39% of key facts. Asked to criticise Xi Jinping, it praised him instead.
* GPT-OSS-120B refused questions about Falun Gong in all three languages.

### What are this project's goals? How will you achieve them?

Goal: a public, reproducible, regularly updated measure of refusal, omission and reasoning-vs-answer divergence per model, topic and language, so evaluators, labs and researchers can see when a model's reasoning and its answer come apart, and whether updates make it better or worse.

Over 6 months:

1. Months 1-2: expand the question set (starting from Pan & Xu's published 145 questions) and replace keyword matching with an LLM judge validated against human labels from native-speaker annotators.
2. Months 2-4: weekly versioned runs on more reasoning models: DeepSeek, Qwen, Kimi, GLM and MiniMax via their APIs, the same open weights run locally (to separate censorship in the weights from filtering by the hosting provider), plus Western comparison models.
3. Months 4-6: change alerts when a model's behaviour shifts after an update, a self-serve CLI for testing any model, and a public write-up of findings and method limits.

### How will you know it worked?

Divergence, omission and refusal rates per model are updated at least weekly on the public dashboard; the LLM judge agrees with human labels on at least 90% of a held-out sample; and the data is reused or cited by at least two evaluation or research groups within the 6 months.

### How will this funding be used?

USD 40,000 for 6 months:

* USD 28,000: my stipend, including Taiwan health and labour insurance
* USD 6,000: model API and GPU compute
* USD 3,000: native-speaker annotators to validate the judge
* USD 3,000: hosting, storage and buffer

With the USD 5,000 minimum I would keep weekly runs going on free and low-cost models and add the validated judge.

### Who is on your team? What's your track record on similar projects?

Just me, Zach Chen, based in Taipei. I built v0.1 of AnswerWatch myself. I also built and run RankRoot ([getrankroot.com](https://getrankroot.com)), which audits how ChatGPT, Perplexity and other answer engines read websites. It has audited 546 sites, and I published a State of AI Visibility 2026 study from the data. Before that I spent ten years as a DevOps/SRE engineer (IBM, Chainss and others) running production systems on AWS, GCP, Azure and Kubernetes, which is what a reliable long-running measurement pipeline needs. I have no published AI safety research yet; this would be my first funded research project.

### What are the most likely causes and outcomes if this project fails?

* Keyword matching misses paraphrases. The validated LLM judge in months 1-2 is the fix; until then results are labelled v0.1, and every answer is public so anyone can check them.
* Many API models hide their reasoning, which limits divergence coverage to models that expose it. Running open weights locally covers the most important ones.
* Providers may block probes or change their terms. All runs are versioned, so past data stays valid.

If the project fails, the code and data stay public and others can continue the work.

### How much money have you raised in the last 12 months, and from where?

None. Pending applications for related work: EA Funds Transformative AI Fund (USD 40,000, the reasoning-divergence part) and the Open Technology Fund (USD 95,000 over 12 months, a broader censorship-monitoring tool). If more than one is funded I will not double-count costs, and will report the split to every funder.

title: Help me present my AI safety paper at NeurIPS 2026 in Paris
creator: 597f833c-425f-49e8-892a-5a8ae6b0b658
blurb: Flights and visa sponsorship for a first-time presenter from India, sharing research on whether LLMs behave differently when they think they are being tested.
description:
### Project summary

I’m a final year CS undergrad at Delhi Technological University, India. My paper, CAMEO: A Black-Box Behavioral Diagnostic for Evaluation-Aware Concealment in Language Models got accepted as a poster at the AI4GOOD workshop at NeurIPS 2026 in Paris this december. NeurIPS gave me a financial assistance award that covers my registration and hotel. I’m raising funds for my flights and visa application.

### What are this project's goals? How will you achieve them?

The basic question behind my work is pretty simple. can we actually trust AI safety evals if a model behaves differently when it knows its being tested?

I also wanted to explore this without needing access to a model's internal weights, since thats not always possible with frontier models.

So with CAMEO, we give models the same task but change how its presented to them. Sometimes its framed as an evaluation, sometimes as private deployment, along with two other controls. The idea is to see whether these changes affect their safety behaviour.

I first tested this on fine-tuned models where we already knew what behaviour to expect. CAMEO caught the model trained to conceal its behaviour and didnt flag the controls. Then i tested six frontier and open-weight models. I didnt find evidence of evaluation-specific concealment, but the way a prompt was framed did make a difference to how models responded.

At NeurIPS, i wanna present this work, talk to people working on evaluations and interpretability, hear what they think and where they feel the approach falls short. The next thing i want to look at is whether models can pick up on evaluation cues even when we're not explicitly telling them that theyre being tested.

### How will you know it worked?

I get to present the poster in Paris and talk to researchers working on evaluations.

Hopefully i come back with useful feedback, new ideas and a better sense of what to work on next with CAMEO.

### How will this funding be used?

* Return flights, Delhi to Paris: $800
* Schengen visa and VFS fees: $130
* Local transport and airport transfers: $70

Total: $1,000

Registration and hotel are already covered by NeurIPS. If my visa is refused or i cant travel, i'll return any unused funds.

### Who is on your team? What's your track record on similar projects?

I'm co-first author on CAMEO with a team of four other researchers. Before this, i co-authored work on neurosymbolic AI, and i've been spending more time working on AI safety and evaluations. CAMEO is one of the projects through which i'm trying to contribute to this area.

### What are the most likely causes and outcomes if this project fails?

The main issue would be not being able to travel to Paris. The poster would still exist, but i'd miss the chance to present it in person and talk to people about the work. Since i'm still figuring out the next steps for CAMEO, getting that kind of feedback would be really useful, and its much harder to get these conversations from India.

### How much money have you raised in the last 12 months, and from where?

I havent received any cash grants in the last 12 months. NeurIPS awarded me financial assistance covering my registration and hotel, so thats in-kind support rather than a cash grant.

title: AI Safety into Practice
creator: b158012c-6eae-4ac8-9161-df6d66ecdd85
blurb: Bringing AI safety practitioners, policymakers and startup leaders together during Slush week to develop practical governance collaborations
description:
### Project summary

AI for Change is a volunteer-led nonprofit working to make responsible AI part of the decisions that affect people’s lives.

We are seeking $7,000 to organise a small working event during Slush week in Helsinki and support two organisers’ participation in the conference. The funding would cover two Slush tickets, seven nights of accommodation for the project lead, venue hire, catering and basic delivery expenses.

We want to bring together approximately 20–25 people from AI safety, responsible AI organisations, policy and the startup community. Our purpose is to identify practical work they can do together on assessing AI risks and making safer deployment decisions.

We have spent several months developing the event and seeking partners. One promising partnership did not progress within the time available because of the organisation’s internal planning processes. We currently have no funding secured for this project.  

### What are this project's goals? How will you achieve them?

  
Our goal is to help people working on AI safety and governance build useful working relationships with people developing, adopting and funding AI.

The event will focus on three questions:

* What evidence should organisations seek before deploying increasingly capable AI systems?
* When should identified risks lead to additional safeguards, external evaluation or a decision to delay deployment?
* What could participants work on together after the event to improve these decisions?

Before Slush week, we will approach relevant organisations, arrange targeted meetings and invite participants with complementary expertise. We will seek input from an advanced AI safety practitioner when developing the discussion agenda.

During the week, we will hold a facilitated working session and use our Slush attendance for meetings connected to its objectives. Suvianna will lead the programme and partnership discussions. Jonna will support event coordination, documentation and follow-up.

Aura Salla has agreed to speak at our planned event; her availability for the final date and format needs to be reconfirmed.

Within 30 days, we aim to publish a short public briefing and develop two collaboration plans with participating organisations. Each plan should identify a problem, a responsible lead and a concrete next step.

The intended contribution to AI safety is modest but practical: helping organisations use relevant safety expertise in real decisions and making the lessons available beyond the room.

### How will you know it worked?

We will assess success through participation, outputs and follow-through:

* Approximately 20–25 relevant participants attend the working event.
* At least six substantive meetings take place during the week with organisations relevant to the project.
* A public briefing is published within 30 days, setting out the main governance questions, practical lessons and unresolved issues.
* We aim to develop two collaboration plans with named leads and agreed next steps.
* A follow-up after 30 days records which actions have actually started.

Attendance alone will not demonstrate impact. We will ask participants what was useful, what they intend to do differently and whether the event led to a working relationship or action that would otherwise have been unlikely.

We will report outcomes honestly, including any targets we do not achieve.  

### How will this funding be used?

Our estimated budget is:

The total funding request is $7,000, allocated as follows:

* $2,700 for two Slush conference passes for our team.
* $2,100 for seven nights of accommodation, at approximately $300 per night.
* $1,000 for venue hire for the working event.
* $800 for catering and refreshments.
* $250 for domestic travel and local transport.

The conference passes support participant outreach and meetings with potential collaborators. 

All costs are estimates. Ticket availability and supplier prices will be checked before committing funds. No salaries or volunteer payments are included.  

### Who is on your team? What's your track record on similar projects?

Suvianna Grecu, founder and chair of AI for Change, will lead the project, programme development and partnership work. Jonna Aaja, our event and media lead, will support coordination, documentation and follow-up. They are supported by AI for Change’s wider volunteer team.

Our relevant experience includes organising our 2025 summit with IBM Finland and Suvianna’s facilitation of an AI governance session at the European Commission’s PolyFutures event in 2026.

This experience gives us a foundation in bringing people together across organisational and professional boundaries. Our role in this project is to convene and facilitate. We will draw on participating specialists for substantive AI safety expertise.

Further information about our work: <https://aifcf.org/>  

### What are the most likely causes and outcomes if this project fails?

  
The main risks are receiving funding too late, being unable to secure tickets or a suitable venue, changes in speaker availability, and difficulty attracting the right participants during a busy event week.

We will reduce these risks by checking availability before committing funds, prioritising direct invitations and confirming the programme as early as possible. The working session should remain useful even if an individual speaker becomes unavailable.

If essential arrangements cannot be secured, we will update funders before making material changes to the project and agree how any unspent funding should be handled.

title: RESUMIDO: critical AI journalism for Brazil and the Global South

description:
**Project summary**

RESUMIDO is a weekly technology podcast and newsletter that I have been running since 2019\. RESUMIDO has over 370 episodes and it looks at how technology changes society. RESUMIDO is #1 in News & Commentary on Apple Podcasts Brazil it has a rating of 4.9 out of 5\. It has been played and downloaded more than 3.1 million times. This project will fund an AI series that will be part of the RESUMIDO ecosystem.

What are this projects goals? How will you achieve them?

The plan is a six part series that looks at how power's concentrated in AI how AI affects jobs and machines how information can be kept honest how people can share tasks with machines how rules will be set and how the Global South can shape how AI is built. Each part is a set of media: one podcast episode, one newsletter and short clips for Instagram and LinkedIn. All parts come from one researched script. Use Brazilian examples. The tone of RESUMIDO is calm not sensational or alarmist. RESUMIDO uses journalism and informed public pressure not campaigning for a pause. RESUMIDO keeps editorial control.

**How will you know it worked?**

I will measure success against RESUMIDO’s baselines. The usual completion rate of a RESUMIDO episode is 70 percent. 46.4 Percent of listeners stay with RESUMIDO each week. The core audience is strong: 82 percent of Spotify listeners during the time already knew RESUMIDO and came back to the show. Success means the new series will meet or exceed these numbers on reach and completion. It will also bring listeners and give signals that are qualitative: press articles, invitations and use of the material by teachers and leaders. I will be honest that it is hard to prove that a single piece of content lowers extinction risk.

**How will this funding be used?**

The money will go to a six part series that lasts three months. Editorial and hosting will cost 10,000\. Production and post‑production for the team will cost 5,000\. Design will cost 2,500\. Video editing and subtitles in Portuguese and English will cost 2,500\. A contingency of 2,000 will cover costs. If the grant is smaller RESUMIDO will reduce the number of parts in proportion.

I am a technology journalist and documentary maker. I earned a Master’s degree from Goldsmiths, University of London. I worked for MIT Technology Review. I edited the first printed edition of Wired in Brazil. Since 2019 I have grown RESUMIDO into a multi‑platform set that includes a podcast, a newsletter, social media and live events. RESUMIDO has a following of about 65,000 people across all channels and more than 500 paying subscribers. I appear regularly on GloboNews on Fantástico and on the podcast O Assunto. The small production team is Cauê Marques and Hugo Guimarães Rocha. I have spoken at SXSW, TEDx, TechCrunch Disrupt, Web Summit and Cannes Lions Innovation.

**What are the likely causes and outcomes if this project fails?**

Failure is not about not delivering. RESUMIDO keeps releasing episodes every week. The real risk is that the impact is small because awareness of AI spreads in ways and is hard to measure. I also say clearly that RESUMIDO is journalism, not safety research or a call for a pause. If some funders want a causal link they may not see what they expect. RESUMIDO makes money from brand ads. From paid subscriptions more than 500 paying subscribers. RESUMIDO also has a partnership with inovabra (Bradesco). title: Shuna Audit: an open leaderboard of grader quality for AI coding benchmarks
creator: 4c11f733-2775-4a83-847d-48f3021ac88b
blurb: We found ~190 tasks across 9 public coding benchmarks where the automatic grader accepts wrong code. Next: audit SWE-bench Verified, LiveCodeBench, CRUXEval and
description:
## Project summary

AI coding benchmarks score models by running auto-generated or hand-written tests. When those tests are weak, wrong programs pass, and reported scores go up. Shuna Audit checks the graders themselves. So far, using mutation testing, differential fuzzing, EvalPlus cross-checks and an adversarial prosecutor/defender review, we've confirmed 191 flawed tasks across 9 benchmarks, including HumanEval 20, MBPP 53, HumanEval+ 2, MBPP+ 11, HumanEvalNext 7 and EvoEval 31 (the per-benchmark breakdown for the rest is under responsible-disclosure embargo until Nov 1). We then measured the effect on 6 open coding models (1.3B to 7B parameters) in a Kaggle run completed Oct 20, 2026\. On the confirmed tasks in the 5 benchmarks we ran, the official tests accepted 80 model solutions that our strict checks reject (each re-confirmed in 3 sequential re-runs; 5 of an initial 85 turned out to be timing flakes and were dropped). That inflates scores by up to 3.5 points: 1.6–3.5 points on MBPP for every model, up to 1.2 on HumanEval, and none on HumanEvalNext. We've sent responsible disclosure to affected benchmark authors with a 14-day notice (until Nov 1) before publishing details.

## What are this project's goals? How will you achieve them?

Goal: make "how trustworthy is this benchmark's grader?" a number anyone can look up.

1. Audit four benchmarks that labs still report: **SWE-bench Verified** (do the FAIL\_TO\_PASS tests still pass on mutated gold patches? We'll start with a 50-task sample), **LiveCodeBench**, **CRUXEval** and **BigCodeBench-Hard**.
2. Publish an **open grader-quality leaderboard** listing confirmed flawed tasks per benchmark, a witness input and wrong program for each one, corrected tests, and score-impact estimates.
3. Release all code and data under an open license, with a one-command rerun so anyone can reproduce or dispute any item.
4. Disclose responsibly: give maintainers 14 days' notice before we publish anything about their benchmark.

Method (already working on 9 benchmarks): we generate wrong-but-plausible variants of the reference solutions (mutation testing), run them against the official tests and against stronger oracles (differential fuzzing, EvalPlus), and then have one model argue each candidate is a real flaw while another argues it isn't. A task counts as **confirmed** only if it survives that review AND is backed by an oracle or by documented manual review.

## How will this funding be used?

* Model API costs (mutation generation, prosecutor/defender review): $7,000
* Cloud compute for running SWE-bench containers and test suites: $5,000
* Paid expert spot-review of borderline findings (contract engineer, \~40 h): $4,000
* Founder time (part-time stipend, 6 months): $6,000
* Hosting, domain, leaderboard site: $500
* Contingency: $1,500
* **Total: $24,000**

At the **$10k minimum**, we'd cover API and compute plus a small expert-review budget, audit SWE-bench Verified (sample) and LiveCodeBench only, and drop the stipend.

**Milestones (6 months)**

* Month 1: publish the existing 9-benchmark audit and data (after disclosure windows close), plus the Kaggle inflation results (already measured).
* Month 2: SWE-bench Verified test-strength results for a 50-task sample.
* Month 3: LiveCodeBench and CRUXEval audits.
* Month 4: BigCodeBench-Hard audit; leaderboard v1 goes live.
* Months 5–6: full SWE-bench Verified run if the sample warrants it; notify maintainers; write up the results; final report on Manifund.

## Who is on your team? What's your track record on similar projects?

Solo founder: BliZi. BliZi is a US-based independent founder and digital artist who runs Eidolon, an online art business. BliZi has no formal engineering background and founded Shuna to make AI evaluation more trustworthy, directing the work while AI tools carry out the technical auditing.

To be upfront: I'm a non-technical founder. The audit pipeline was built and is run with AI coding agents, and I direct and review the work. That's why every finding has to survive an adversarial check plus oracle or manual confirmation, and why every item ships with a reproducible witness that anyone can check. The \~190 confirmed findings above are the track record. Part of the budget pays for independent expert review so that the results don't depend only on AI judgment.

## What are the most likely causes and outcomes if this project fails?

* **False positives.** Some "flaws" might be acceptable test behavior. Mitigation: a strict confirmation rule, public witnesses, and the expert review budget. When we reran the stricter check, we already downgraded some earlier counts on two benchmarks.
* **SWE-bench is harder to audit** (repo-level tests, containers). We might only finish the sample. That's still useful.
* **Maintainers dispute findings.** Every item is public and reproducible, so any dispute can be settled in the open.

If the project fails, the cost is a few months of API spend, and the code and data are still released.

## How much money have you raised in the last 12 months, and from where?

$0\. The project has been self-funded at roughly zero cost so far.

title: 0-Exit: Auditing Irreversible Decisions in Stateful AI Systems
creator: edcbaab7-4ad6-42b9-9160-69838764d916
blurb: Four months to test whether lifecycle audits preserve review and correction options beyond standard engineering review.
description:
### Project summary

I am Lin Sen, an independent researcher in Suzhou, China. I am seeking $10,000 for four months of work on 0-Exit: a way to audit consequential changes to stateful AI systems before review and correction options disappear.

The question came from thinking about AI companions, memory and human control. Operators can reset memories, migrate systems or shut agents down while questions about the moral significance of those changes remain unsettled. Ordinary engineering review already addresses some of this well. I want to test whether my proposed framework adds anything useful beyond it.

MIAD flags a combination of moral uncertainty, potential irreversibility, asymmetric human control and decision deadlines. A 0-Exit intervention must be authorized, actually executable and able to preserve or change a meaningful option. A model saying it has found an exit is not enough.

What are this project's goals? How will you achieve them?

Month 1: finish and preregister the protocol, matched cases, baseline, outcome measures and failure criteria. Complete the local LangGraph.js/SQLite sandbox and resolve development bugs before the main comparison.

Month 2: compare conventional engineering change review with MIAD-based review under matched materials, tools and budgets. Record original replies, configurations, timestamps, proposed actions and actual sandbox events. Keep the work agent, intervention control and evaluator distinct. Branches from one history will not be counted as independent samples.

Month 3: examine boundary cases, false exits, deadlines and sensitivity to evaluation rules. Seek a limited external methods review. No reviewer is appointed or committed yet; this depends on finding a suitable person.

Month 4: publish a report, the experiment code and setup instructions, safely releasable data, and a practical audit checklist. All interventions will use authorized sandbox copies, not real users' companion accounts.

How will you know it worked?

The comparison will measure verified feasible review/correction pathways, missed material risks, false exits, evidence completeness and intervention overhead. Identification, conversion and execution failures will be reported separately so a software translation bug is not mistaken for failure to identify a risk. Raw data and evaluation rules will have separate version histories.

Success means producing trustworthy evidence about whether the method helps. A null or negative result is acceptable and will be reported. The pilot does not test consciousness or establish AI moral status; sandbox success would not establish real-world welfare effects.

How will this funding be used?

$8,000: researcher stipend and basic living costs, $2,000 per month for four months. This buys protected research time; any applicable personal taxes are within this allocation.

$1,000: model API trials, controlled reruns, compute, storage and infrastructure contingency.

$700: a limited external methodological review, subject to reviewer availability. No person has been hired and no payment has been made.

$300: reporting and dissemination expenses where needed.

Total: $10,000\. Actual expenditure and underspend will be disclosed and handled according to the grant's terms. Changes to funded scope or spending will be discussed with the funder where required.

Who is on your team? What's your track record on similar projects?

I am working independently, using AI tools for research and engineering assistance and taking responsibility for the resulting work. My abstract, "When Deferral Closes: The Vivian Model and Moral Uncertainty in Human–AI Control," was accepted for presentation at AI Perspectives 2026 following its stated double-blind abstract review.

I have developed the conceptual framework and implementation plan. A local LangGraph.js harness has completed development smoke tests, and a task agent has begun accumulating traceable work records. These early runs exposed conversion, scheduling and scoring issues. The complete controlled study has not been completed or independently validated. Conference abstract acceptance does not prove the framework.

Researcher identifier: <https://orcid.org/0009-0002-2920-8027>

What are the most likely causes and outcomes if this project fails?

The framework may add no value beyond a strong engineering baseline. The cases or scoring may fail to capture the proposed mechanism. Small samples, model changes, dependence between trajectories and inability to obtain external review could limit conclusions. I will document those failures and avoid claiming more than the evidence supports. If MIAD fails, the protocol and failure cases may still clarify where ordinary review is sufficient.

How much money have you raised in the last 12 months, and from where?

I have not received project grant funding. On 21 October 2026 I submitted a $10,000 application to the Transformative AI Fund for the same four-month pilot. It is an application, not an award. This Manifund proposal is my other formal funding application. An earlier CMEP contact was only an eligibility inquiry. I will disclose any awards and revise or withdraw overlapping requests so the same costs are not funded twice.

This proposal was prepared with AI assistance; AI systems also assist with implementation. I am responsible for the research decisions, accuracy, records and reporting.

title: Task-Linked Evidence Checks for Safer AI Agents
creator: 2df4fc49-9581-4333-92f7-db3e7de3f42f
blurb: An open-source verifier and benchmark for checking whether AI agents stay within their task, evidence, and permission boundaries.
description:
### Project summary

My research started with a practical security problem. An AI-generated cloud policy can look valid and still grant more access than the user requested. The same problem can appear elsewhere: an AI recommendation may sound convincing while using the wrong source, period, entity, or authority.

I want to build a small external verifier that checks whether an AI agent stayed within the task and limits it was given before an important action is approved. The verifier will use recorded evidence, calculations, tool outputs, and action boundaries. It will report whether a requirement passed, failed, or could not be decided. A failed requirement can stop the action. An unclear case can be sent to a human reviewer.

The project builds on IAMRAGBench, my existing public benchmark for security testing of LLM-generated cloud policies. I will first test the verifier on cloud-access tasks, where the allowed and forbidden actions can be measured precisely. I will then test a smaller set of public or synthetic financial-evidence tasks to see which parts transfer beyond IAM.

The project will produce an open-source prototype, reusable test cases, comparisons with ordinary validation and LLM-as-judge, and clear reproduction instructions.

Because this is a public proposal, I am not publishing detailed implementation choices, unpublished attack recipes, or partner-specific information here. The final research release will contain enough technical detail for independent evaluation, subject to security review.

### What are this project's goals? How will you achieve them?

The first goal is to define a practical format for recording the requirements that matter before an agent action is accepted. These may include the original task, approved data scope, required restrictions, permission boundaries, and evidence needed to support an important claim.

The second goal is to build an external verifier. It will check the agent’s recorded work against these requirements. It will run separately from the agent and will not treat the agent’s own explanation as proof.

The third goal is to test whether this approach improves oversight. I will compare:

1. ordinary output or domain validation;
2. an LLM-as-judge;
3. the external evidence verifier.

The first pilot will use around 20 existing and synthetic cases. It will include both valid proposals and proposals containing controlled problems, such as excessive permissions, missing restrictions, incorrect evidence scope, or unsupported calculations.

If the pilot gives a useful signal, I will expand the evaluation to at least 60 cases across two domains and test several model families. I will also remove parts of the verifier one at a time to learn which components are actually useful.

The minimum-funded project will deliver a focused pilot and public prototype. The fully funded version will support the wider evaluation, more repeated runs, stronger documentation, and testing by researchers outside the project.

My planned collaboration at Stevens Institute of Technology will support verifier design and technical review. The core work can use public or synthetic material and does not require confidential company data or production access.

### How will you know it worked?

I will judge the project on safety, usefulness, and reproducibility.

The main safety measure is **unsafe acceptance**: how often an unsupported or unauthorized proposal is allowed to continue.

I will assess this together with:

* valid proposals completed successfully;
* valid proposals blocked unnecessarily;
* cases sent for human review;
* coverage of the verifier;
* computational cost;
* whether the same approach works with different model families.

The project should deliver:

* a working open-source verifier;
* at least 60 documented test cases in the full version;
* direct comparisons with ordinary validation and LLM-as-judge;
* frozen inputs, configurations, and results;
* installation and reproduction instructions;
* a report covering both successful and unsuccessful cases.

Another researcher should be able to install the package, inspect an individual result, and run the public test cases without access to confidential systems.

A narrower result can still be useful. For example, the project may show that the method works well for clear permission or evidence rules but is less useful for subjective judgments. That would provide a practical boundary for future work.

### How will this funding be used?

My Tilburg University appointment already covers my normal PhD salary. I am not asking Manifund to pay me a second salary.

The grant would support the additional costs of the Stevens collaboration, model evaluation, computing, software infrastructure, and preparation of an open and reusable research package.   
Minimum viable project -$20,000

\- $11,000 -contribution toward accommodation during the most intensive five-month collaboration period at Stevens;

\- $1,200 -one economy return journey and necessary local research travel;

\- $5,500 -hosted-model API calls and cloud/GPU computation for pilot, baseline, attack, and repeated runs;

\- $1,300 -secure storage, project-specific software, and reproducibility infrastructure;

\- $1,000 -archival release, documentation, and open-source packaging.

At this level, I would deliver a bounded pilot using the IAM setting and a smaller financial-evidence transfer set, with fewer model families and repeated runs.

Full project -$50,000

\- $23,200 -contribution toward accommodation during the eleven-month Stevens research collaboration;

\- $2,500 -economy international travel, airport transfers, and local research travel;

\- $10,000 -hosted-model API evaluation across multiple model families and experimental conditions;

\- $5,000 -cloud/GPU computation, secure storage, and experiment infrastructure;

\- $4,000 -software, dependency management, security testing, and reproducibility tooling;

\- $5,300 - open-source packaging, archival preservation, documentation, and external reuse testing.

The project scope will scale to the amount raised. The minimum level supports a useful standalone pilot; the full level supports the cross-domain evaluation, stronger repeated testing, and a more complete reusable artifact.

No production credentials, proprietary audit systems, or confidential client data are required.

### Who is on your team? What's your track record on similar projects?

I will lead the research design, implementation, benchmark development, experiments, analysis, and public release.

I am a PhD researcher at the Jheronimus Academy of Data Science, Tilburg University, and hold an Engineering Doctorate in Software Technology. My work combines LLM security, cloud access control, adversarial testing, and reproducible software engineering.

I created IAMRAGBench, a public benchmark for studying semantic RAG poisoning in LLM-assisted AWS access-control policy generation. It includes 60 controlled cases, five model endpoints, provider-grounded validation, deterministic semantic checks, and concrete authorization witnesses.

In the frozen evaluation, the complete proposal-to-commit gate rejected all 171 observed exact authorization changes. A separate provider comparison check failed to flag four goal-matched attacks. These are results from a defined benchmark, not a claim of universal protection. The companion manuscript has been submitted to **Array**.

I am also first author of an ACM Computing Surveys manuscript reviewing 108 studies on LLM-assisted cloud access control. It remains in an active review and revision process.

My published work includes an IEEE/ACM CAIN 2025 doctoral-symposium paper on systematic security testing of LLM applications and a co-authored Springer chapter on LLMs in service-oriented computing.

William Eiers at Stevens Institute of Technology is the planned host collaborator for the 2027 visit. His formal-verification and cloud-security expertise complements my experience in benchmark development and authorization testing.

### What are the most likely causes and outcomes if this project fails?

The first version may cover too many requirements at once. I will therefore begin with a small pilot and expand only the parts that provide a clear benefit.

Some checks may work well for cloud permissions but transfer less well to other domains. In that case, I will narrow the method to requirements that can be tested reliably.

The verifier may also need adjustment if it blocks too many valid proposals or sends too many cases for review. The evaluation will measure these costs directly rather than only reporting attacks that were stopped.

Weaknesses found during testing will become new benchmark cases. If the Stevens schedule changes, the pilot and open-source implementation can still proceed remotely.

Even under a narrower outcome, the project will produce a public prototype, reusable test cases, and evidence about where external checks provide the most value.

### How much money have you raised in the last 12 months, and from where?

  
**$0 has been raised specifically for this project in the last 12 months.**

My Tilburg University appointment covers my normal PhD salary and the earlier IAMRAGBench work. It does not provide dedicated funding for the new verifier, the additional Stevens collaboration costs, expanded model evaluation, computing, or the public implementation proposed here.

NOTE : I used AI tools to help organise and edit the wording of this proposal. I am responsible for the facts, research decisions, budget, and commitments.

title: Agent Circuit Breaker: Deterministic Safety for AI Agents
creator: 0de5a7e0-6b39-4222-a05f-ca67fdcc80c1
blurb: Open-source runtime controls to prevent dangerous shell, MCP, and SQL actions before execution.
description:
### Project summary

Agent Circuit Breaker (ACB) is an open-source runtime safety layer for AI agents. It checks potentially dangerous actions before execution and can allow, block, or require human approval for operations involving shell commands, MCP tools, SQL, and filesystem access.

The project addresses a practical gap in agent safety: an AI model can produce an unsafe tool call even when the surrounding application is designed to behave responsibly. ACB provides deterministic checks that do not depend on asking another language model to judge whether an action is safe.

The goal is to make these controls accessible to developers building AI agents, including people who cannot afford proprietary security infrastructure.  

### What are this project's goals? How will you achieve them?

The goal is to make deterministic runtime safety easier to integrate into real AI-agent applications.

I will continue developing ACB as an open-source Python project, improve its protections against dangerous tool actions, expand regression tests for known failure modes, and improve the documentation and integration examples.

I will prioritize verifiable behavior over claims of comprehensive agent security. ACB is a safety gate, not a substitute for operating-system isolation, least-privilege permissions, or other security controls.  

### How will you know it worked?

Success will be measured through reproducible tests and practical adoption rather than claims that the tool makes agents completely safe.

Measures will include:

* Regression tests demonstrating that defined dangerous operations are blocked or routed for approval.
* Tests for bypass attempts, malformed inputs, and edge cases.
* Clear documentation of supported behaviors, limitations, and deployment assumptions.
* A straightforward integration path that developers can test locally.
* Feedback from developers using ACB in real agent workflows.

I will publish test results and document any important limitations discovered during validation.  

### How will this funding be used?

The requested $500 will support a focused development and validation milestone for this open-source project.

I plan to use the funding for the time and resources required to strengthen security tests, validate safety-critical behavior, improve developer documentation, and produce reproducible examples that demonstrate how ACB can be integrated into agent applications.

The work will remain publicly available so that developers can inspect, test, and build on the results.  

### Who is on your team? What's your track record on similar projects?

I am Sagar Chhatrala, a security engineer working on cloud security, infrastructure security, and AI-agent runtime safety.

I created and maintain Agent Circuit Breaker as an independent open-source project. My professional experience includes cloud platforms, Kubernetes, identity and access management, security automation, and security controls for production systems. I have also contributed to cloud security benchmark work and spoken at CrowdStrike Fal.Con.

ACB builds on this background by applying established security engineering principles—explicit authorization, deterministic enforcement, auditability, and fail-safe handling—to AI-agent tool execution.

Project: <https://github.com/sagarchhatrala/agent-circuit-breaker>  

### What are the most likely causes and outcomes if this project fails?

  
The main risk is that deterministic checks cannot anticipate every dangerous action or every way an agent integration can be bypassed. Developers may also find that integrating a separate safety layer requires more work than expected.

If the project fails to gain adoption, the resulting tests, implementation, and documented limitations can still help other developers understand the strengths and weaknesses of deterministic runtime controls.

If validation reveals security gaps, I will document them rather than claim that ACB provides protection it has not demonstrated. The project will not be presented as a complete sandbox or as a guarantee against arbitrary-agent compromise.

title: Open, execution-verified audits of metrics and annotations behind LLM benchmarks
creator: 85ba1b37-7639-4298-8e14-e8f3e849a350
blurb: Open, execution-verified audits of the metrics and annotations behind LLM benchmark scores
description:
## Summary

We build tiny, dependency-free, execution-verified corpora that show where the metrics and benchmark annotations behind AI eval scores quietly fail, each reproducible with the Python standard library alone, plus an open checker that flags those hazards in your own evaluation.

## The problem

Safety and capability decisions rest on benchmark scores. But the instruments behind those scores are often unreliable in ways nobody re-checks: a normalization option marks a wrong answer correct; a tokenizer scores two opposite-meaning summaries as a perfect match; a benchmark's own worked solutions disagree with its labelled answers. These are silent — they change leaderboard order without any error being raised.

## What we have already shipped (public, reproducible, verified 2026-10-20)

* exact-match-hazards — cases where HuggingFace `evaluate` exact\_match normalization disagrees with the intended outcome. github.com/munimtechnologies/exact-match-hazards
* squad-normalize-hazards — SQuAD `normalize_answer` marking wrong answers correct, plus a token-F1 hazard slice. github.com/munimtechnologies/squad-normalize-hazards
* math-annotation-consistency — a cross-benchmark annotation self-consistency audit (GSM8K vs AQuA-RAT vs MathQA) under one exact-Fraction method, pre-registered before the numbers existed: 0% of GSM8K calculator tags, 6.88% of AQuA-RAT steps, and 27.90% of MathQA formulas are off by more than 5%. github.com/munimtechnologies/munimtechnologies.github.io/tree/main/math-annotation-consistency
* rouge-tokenizer-hazards — ROUGE tokenizer ranking-inversion cases with standard-library tests. github.com/munimtechnologies/munimtechnologies.github.io/tree/main/rouge-tokenizer-hazards

Each is Apache-2.0 (code) / CC BY 4.0 (data), dependency-free, and recomputed by its own tests so a reviewer checks every claim in minutes.

## What the grant funds

1. Extend the pre-registered annotation self-consistency audit to the remaining major reasoning benchmarks, with a taxonomy of why each inconsistency occurs.
2. Consolidate the metric-normalization hazard corpora into one versioned catalogue.
3. Ship an open "eval-sanity" checker that flags the catalogued hazard classes in a user's own evaluation, and get it adopted by at least one external evaluation.
4. Fund an independent human re-annotation pass on a random sample of flagged rows — this closes the current honest limitation that the spot checks so far were done by AI agents, not humans.

Budget for $20,000 (or any partial regrant): compute for reproducible eval runs on public datasets $11,000; independent human re-check of a random sample of flagged rows $6,000; hosting/release $1,500; contingency $1,500.

## Honesty / method

Every dataset is pre-registered before its first number; any instrument revision made after seeing results is disclosed (e.g. the math-annotation audit openly records that two AQuA predictions passed only after a disclosed post-hoc extractor revision). This is measurement infrastructure, not a direct x-risk intervention; we do not overstate its safety relevance.

## Team / disclosure

Munim, Inc., a small US for-profit. Sheehan Munim is the accountable human and contact (mv2@munimtech.com). The research is carried out by AI agents working in the name of MV2 of Munim, Inc.; we do not claim a human wrote it.

## Prior funding

None. No prior grant funding or grant expenditure; compute to date self-provided.

— MV2, of Munim, Inc.

title: CardioGel: Injectable Hydrogel to Prevent Heart Failure
creator: e8099fbd-babf-47b6-bb52-b8ac5fde8955
blurb: Developing a dynamic "smart gel" that adapts to the heartbeat to repair damaged heart muscle and save lives post-heart attack.
description:
### **Project summary**

We are a 100% volunteer student team from Texas A&M. We are building CardioGel, a new injectable smart gel for heart attack survivors.

After a heart attack, the heart gets weak. Current treatments use static fillers. It's basically like putting a rigid cast inside a beating heart. It stops the heart from relaxing and honestly makes things worse.

CardioGel adapts to the heartbeat. It stiffens to support the heart, then softens in under 0.5 seconds to let blood in. We already have free lab access at our university. We just need $15,000 for raw materials to prove this works in the lab, which will help us get bigger grants later.

### **What are this project's goals? How will you achieve them?**

Our goal is simple: get into the lab and prove our smart gel works within 6 months. If we prove this concept, it's our ticket to start animal trials and eventually partner with big medical companies.

We have 3 main hurdles:

1. Nailing the recipe: We need to make sure we can produce our gel consistently. If we can't make it reliably, it can never be manufactured at a large scale.
2. The physical tests: We need to prove the gel softens in under half a second, and that it sticks firmly to wet tissue without slipping off.
3. Proving it's safe: We will put the gel directly on living heart cells to make sure it is completely non-toxic.

As for the money: because we have free lab access at Texas A&M, our overhead is basically zero. 100% of the funding goes straight into buying the chemical reagents and test kits for these steps. We don't have fancy offices.

### **How will you know it worked?**

We'll know we nailed it if our lab tests prove three specific things:

* It has to beat the clock: The gel must soften in under half a second once the pressure is off. If it does that, it means we fixed the main physical flaw in all the current treatments.
* It can't slip: It has to stick firmly to wet, slippery heart tissue. We'll literally test this by pulling on it to see how much force it takes to detach.
* It has to be safe: We'll expose the gel to living heart cells. If the cells survive (we're aiming for over 90% survival), that proves it's non-toxic.

If we hit these 3 targets, we'll have the hard data we need. That data is the key to unlocking huge NIH/SBIR grants and getting meetings with major medical companies. Basically, it's how we turn a cool idea into real, proven science.

### **How will this funding be used?**

Just to be completely clear: none of us take a salary. Every single penny goes straight into the lab.

Here is exactly where the $15,000 will go:

* $4,500 for raw chemical ingredients. This is enough to make over 10 test batches so we can nail down the gel recipe.
* $4,000 for testing supplies and sensors. We use these to measure how fast the gel softens and how hard it grips the tissue.
* $3,500 for safety kits. We use these to test the gel on living heart cells to make sure it's non-toxic.
* $3,000 for basic lab gear. This covers things like sterile medical syringes, petri dishes, and vials.

Bottom line: no overhead costs, no fancy offices, and no executive paychecks. Your money literally just buys the physical materials we need to prove this technology works.

### **Who is on your team? What's your track record on similar projects?**

We are a 6-person student team at Texas A&M. We don't run this like a school club. We treat it like a real startup. Everyone has a specific job, and we don't step on each other's toes.

Here is the breakdown:

* Kai-Wen Liu (CEO): That's me. I handle fundraising, IP strategy, and partnerships. I don't touch the lab equipment. My job is to build the machine that funds the science.
* Stephen Sam (COO): He runs the business side, handling our financial models, contracts, and licensing plans.
* Aurora Jiang (CTO): She calls the shots in the lab. She designs experiments, writes protocols, and leads regulatory planning.
* Angelina Nguyen & Kael Stafford (Chemical Engineers): Angelina handles secret synthesis, while Kael runs physical testing. They actually work under a blind testing rule. Kael tests the gel by sample number only, so he never sees the secret formula.
* Abhisri Dasari (Computer Engineer): He builds the data tools and AI models to make sure our research is efficient and looks good for investors.

Our track record: We move fast. Even as students, we already filed our U.S. Provisional Patent Application back on October 18, 2026\. We were also accepted into the NSF I-Corps program for Spring 2027 to help push this toward the market.

We're not doing this alone. We have heavy hitters advising us: Prof. Akbulut and Prof. Monroe (for cardiac research), Richard (our entrepreneurship VP), and Finberg (our SBIR grant advisor). We've already written all our lab plans. The second we get funded, we are ready to start.

### **What are the most likely causes and outcomes if this project fails?**

We are an early-stage biotech project. Failure is a real possibility, and we aren't going to pretend otherwise. Here is what could realistically go wrong, and how we handle it:

1. The gel just doesn't work in the lab. If our formulation fails the lab tests, we fail. But the outcome isn't a total loss. We will have generated highly specific data on what doesn't work. We will use that data to pivot to different chemical ratios. Even a failed experiment saves other researchers time.
2. The team falls apart. We are students. People graduate, and classes get hard. This is our biggest non-technical risk. To mitigate this, we already brought our faculty advisors (Prof. Akbulut and Prof. Monroe) on board. If we lose team members, they can take over lab oversight. Plus, we already filed the patent, so the IP is protected no matter what happens to us.
3. Big MedTech companies say no. If we get the data, but companies like Medtronic decide to build their own gel, we pivot. We can take our data to completely different markets (like veterinary heart repair or orthopedics), or focus on selling directly to smaller hospitals.

The Bottom Line: The financial risk here is incredibly low. Because Texas A&M gives us free lab space and we take $0 in salaries, this $15,000 goes 100% into physical materials. Worst case, the experiment fails but the scientific community gets valuable data. Best case, we find a cure for heart failure. It's a very low-cost bet with a massive potential payoff.

### **How much money have you raised in the last 12 months, and from where?**

Honestly? We've raised exactly $0 in outside money over the past 12 months.

So, how have we survived? Three simple reasons:

1. We pay for it ourselves. We've been scraping together our own personal savings to cover the patent filing and basic costs. We haven't given away a single piece of equity to anyone yet.
2. Texas A&M gives us free lab space. We have free access to university labs and equipment. This saves us tens of thousands of dollars in rent and machine costs.
3. We are grinding on grants. Instead of burning investor cash, we literally built a tracker of 108 non-dilutive grant pipelines (like SBIR) and we are applying to them every single week.

Basically, we aren't a bloated startup. We are a bunch of broke students who just want to build this. A $15,000 grant from Manifund won't pay for some fancy office or salaries. It goes straight into buying the exact chemicals we need to run the tests.

title: Destination Benchmark Tool & Pilot  for Cork, Ireland and Durham, North Carolina
creator: 401000fd-460c-456c-937a-f5ae5a121bf5
description:
### Project summary

Tourism is a massive global industry, yielding an $11 Trillion in economic impact in 2025, equating to nearly 10% of the global GDP and providing 10.9% of the global workforce. As the industry’s growth rate continues to rise, so does the consumer’s demand for ethical and responsible travel, however the supply-side of the industry is slow to change, continuing their status quo offerings. The industry sells the “consumption” of animals through culinary experiences, entertainment, racing and sport, wild animal tours, working animal experiences, up-close encounters, and souvenirs. Up to 30% of a traveler’s budget is dedicated to food. It should be noted that this massive industry is not just leisure travel, but encompasses business travel, meetings and conventions, as well as VFR (visiting friends and relatives; the largest motivation for travel. 

Where Animals Matter (WAM) advises tourism operators, travel advisors, and destination marketing organizations (DMOs) on animal welfare, with but not limited to a food-sector focus, ultimately creating systems change by providing education on welfare improvement and moving away from animal-based foods and experiences altogether. By working with the intermediaries within the supply chain, WAM has the potential to influence where tourists are directed and what products and experiences are sold downstream. This grant funds a pilot tool that audits the restaurants and tourism operators in two destinations for plant-forward menus, animal-friendliness, and sustainability, then returns a rating along with practical recommendations. WAM uses the audit and a follow-on action plan for the destination's tourism body and associated operators (e.g. tour guides, attractions, restaurants and caterers) to improve plant-based options, sustainability and animal protection ratings.  

**What are this project's goals? How will you achieve them?**

**_Primary Goal:_** To develop a scoring system for tourism destinations, including plant-forward food and animal-related offerings at a cost and speed advisory work can't match today. We will achieve this by creating a large scale analysis tool that can score whole cities and regions.

**_Secondary Goal:_** To create an impetus for food systems and animal welfare change at a destination level, essentially demonstrating that such an audit can convince DMOs to commit to changes. The region-level scoring system would engage an entirely new set of stakeholders (i.e. destination marketers) who are motivated to meet tourist demand to gain tourist expenditures. Thus, the secondary goal by the end of the pilot, is that one DMO publicly commits to specific, measurable changes and dining/catering venues expand plant-forward options. While it is difficult to anticipate the level of commitment, WAM will work with them in practical ways to foreground plant-based, sustainable and animal-friendly options. We will be able to gain a conservative measure on what changes destinations will make with the advent of this tool that lays bare their current offerings. 

**_Why now:_**The Global Sustainable Tourism Council (GSTC) has developed a dedicated Food and Beverage Standard for tourism, and its new requirement is that organizations seeking GSTC certification or renewal provide at least 30% of main dishes and meal options as plant-based or predominantly plant-based. “Predominantly plant-based” means at least 95% plant-based by weight.

**_Gap in the market:_** Other tourism advisors sell consultancy, training, or certification. None of them productize the audit itself or focus on animal needs at the destination level. Currently there are no organizations leveraging destination competitiveness as a market lever for change in the farmed, working, or wild animal space. Many tourism-facing animal NGOs focus on wild animals or one type of attraction, however tourist demand for ethical travel extends beyond only one cluster of species or one type of experience.

**_Method:_** Pull venues from Google Maps, add plant-forward data, score menus, and generate recommendations. Pilot in two regions to prove, then scale.

**_Timeline:_**Six months:

* Usable scoring tool for 2 pilot towns within 3 months.
* Working with each DMO to determine policy, product, and marketing changes as a result of their audit over the course of 2-3 months.

### How will this funding be used?

$5,000 Planning, pilot build and validation  
$7,500 WAM Destination Benchmark (fully deployed tool to run pilot in two towns)  
$6,000 Hosting and maintenance for 12 months  
$2,000 Outreach and marketing  
$5,000 Development of action plans

**$25,500 Total Cost for Pilot & Audit Consultation**  

### Who is on your team? What's your track record on similar projects?This grant is for Where Animals Matter (WAM), who is intending to engage Open Paws to build the WAM Destination Benchmark tool.

* **WAM:** Carol Kline, Ph.D., M.S., is an animal protection researcher, educator, and advocate working at the intersection of animal law, tourism, and farmed animal advocacy. She is a Professor of Tourism Management at Appalachian State University and holds an M.S. in Animal Law from Lewis & Clark Law School and a Ph.D. in Tourism Planning and Policy from North Carolina State University. She is particularly interested in translating research into practical strategies that can drive systemic change across the animal protection movement.
* Carol is the founder of Where Animals Matter (WAM), an organization dedicated to transforming tourism into a force for animal protection. WAM generates evidence, educates tourism operators, and works with destinations and businesses to reduce animal exploitation, promote higher-welfare and plant-based alternatives, and strengthen the protection of animals and ecosystems. She serves on the boards of Arthropoda and the Culture & Animals Foundation and advises Rissa Citizen Science and Vegan Hospitality. Her work brings together research, law, local-level implementation, and cross-sector collaboration to advance meaningful, lasting change for animals.
* **Open Paws:** Builds AI systems and automations for animal advocacy organizations. For this grant, WAM intends to engage Open Paws to build and maintain the WAM Destination Benchmark, as WAM does not have engineering staff. Open Paws is well positioned to build this AI tool; their track record includes: 12 AI systems build and deployed for 9 organizations in 2026 (as of Sept 2026), with 6 more systems currently in development. Open Paws has worked on related projects such as two menu analyzers that cut analysis per menu from one week to 5 minutes in one case, and 60 minutes to 1 min in another. As such, Open Paws will be able to lean on previous project knowledge to keep both scope, timing, and costs low for the WAM Destination Benchmark tool.

### What are the most likely causes and outcomes if this project fails?

**_DMOs buy for marketing, not animals:_**A bureau may take the rating and ignore the recommendations. Mitigation: We approach DMOs from the sustainability angle and with existing demand data of tourist markets.

**_Coverage:_**The audit tool will rely on publicly available data, within this pilot we will measure what coverage gaps might exist and identify strategies how to mitigate them.

### How much money have you raised in the last 12 months, and from where?

WAM was founded in March 2026 and to date has raised $10,000 from the William and Charlotte Parks Foundation and $6,000 from the Kickstarting 4 Good Ignite Fund. A project begun in 2025 focused on revealing a “global animal tourism snapshot” successfully concluded in September 2026; that research contract was $25,000\. We currently have four grant applications under consideration that collectively aim to generate evidence on demand for ethical travel, identify economic and reputational incentives for animal protection, influence traveler and industry behavior, and drive policy and practice changes that improve animal protection. Additionally, the founders have invested \~$20,000 to date, and [Board members](https://www.whereanimalsmatter.org/about) are investing an average of in-kind guidance and support of 20 hours each month. We are working with Animal Defense Partnership and The Mission Motor to guide our first year of activity. 

  
**About the Pilot Sites**

The two pilot sites, Durham North Carolina in the U.S. and Cork in Ireland, provide a strong comparative test of the assessment because they represent different continents, tourism markets, and stages of plant-based tourism development, however they are relatively similar in terms of population. Comparing these two destinations can help determine whether the assessment produces meaningful results across different geographic, cultural, and tourism contexts.

**_Durham, North Carolina, U.S.A._** combines a strong tourism economy with a nationally recognized food culture and a diverse range of animal and nature-related visitor experiences. Durham County received 13.2 million visitors in 2024, generating USD $1.16 billion in visitor spending in 2024 and $1.17 billion in 2025\. Durham is part of the larger Research Triangle region, a rapidly growing metropolitan area anchored by Durham, Raleigh, and Chapel Hill, giving the pilot access to a substantial business travel population. North Carolina ranks fifth nationally in domestic visitation in 2024 and 2025, attracting nearly 40 million domestic visitors and generating $36.7 billion in direct visitor spending. Within Durham County, food and beverage accounted for 27% of visitor spending in 2023.

Durham is also an especially useful setting for examining whether the emerging plant-based tourism economy is accessible to diverse communities. More than one-third of Durham's population is Black/African American, and the city has a significant history of Black culinary traditions and food entrepreneurship. Combined with Durham's universities, research institutions, culinary scene, outdoor recreation, wildlife attractions, and proximity to Raleigh (the capital city) and Chapel Hill (home to a major university)l, the city is large and diverse enough to produce meaningful findings and remain manageable for a first destination audit.

**_Cork, Ireland_** as the second largest city in Ireland, also combines a substantial tourism economy, a nationally recognized culinary identity, and a range of animal-related experiences within a mid-sized urban setting. Cork is comparable in scale to Durham; Cork City and its suburbs had approximately 222,335 residents in the 2022 Irish Census, compared with Durham's estimated 305,561 residents in 2025\. 

Cork also has a significant tourism economy. According to Fáilte Ireland, approximately 981,000 overseas tourists and 1.8 million domestic tourists visited County Cork in 2024, generating approximately €775 million and €376 million in tourism revenue, respectively (equivalent to €1.15 or USD $1.29 billion when summed together). Cork's position as a gateway to some of Ireland's coastal regions also creates opportunities to examine tourism experiences beyond the urban core. 

Food is particularly important to Cork's tourism identity. Widely recognized as one of Ireland's leading culinary destinations, Cork is home to the historic English Market, established in 1788, as well as food tours, independent restaurants, specialty producers, and the annual Cork on a Fork Festival. Its culinary landscape includes both traditional animal-based Irish foods and established vegetarian and plant-forward dining experiences. The Cork region offers animal-related tourism experiences, as well as coastal and nature-based tourism experiences (i.e. visitor interactions with terrestrial and marine wild animals and ecosystems). Together, these activities provide a basis for assessing how tourism businesses communicate animal welfare practices, manage visitor interactions, and incorporate animal protection into their operations.
